    Google’s Expansion Of Personal Intelligence Will Change SEO via @sejournal, @martinibuster

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google revealed the expansion of its Personal Intelligence feature.
    • Google’s announcement explains the connection to Search:.
    • “The most helpful search experience brings together the richness of the world’s information with insights uniquely relevant to you.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google revealed the expansion of its Personal Intelligence feature. The expansion unifies many of Google’s disparate products and services into a single personalized search experience. This revision represents a profound change to Google’s Search experience and is likely among the most consequential changes to SEO.

    Google’s announcement explains the connection to Search:.

    “The most helpful search experience brings together the richness of the world’s information with insights uniquely relevant to you. Today, Search is getting even more tailored with the ability to connect more of your apps to Personal Intelligence — and we’re introducing more personally relevant responses, so it’s easier to find just what you need.”.

    It has been revealed that some SEOs objected to characterizing Personal Intelligence as something that is about Search, explaining that Personal Intelligence is about Gemini, AI Mode, and AI Overviews. That view can be justified because Google’s announcement is somewhat ambiguous.

    Industry observers note that google’s announcement uses the upper-case word Search sixteen times. That seems to be a clear signal that Personal Intelligence affects Search.

    “A more tailored Google Search that’s uniquely yours….

    …Get more helpful Search responses….

    …Today, Search is getting even more tailored with the ability to connect more of your apps to Personal Intelligence….

    …bringing context from your spending, documents, and chats directly to Search.”.

    The following passage seems to unambiguously paint the rollout as affecting Search:.

    “Starting to roll out today, you can opt in to securely connect Google Wallet to Personal Intelligence in AI Mode, with support for Drive and the Gemini app following in the coming weeks — bringing context from your spending, documents, and chats directly to Search.”.

    The above passage clearly separates AI Mode from Search. Yet, other passages reference AI Mode in Search, introducing a certain amount of ambiguity. An argument can be made that this does not affect Search, but there’s a strong counter-argument there, too.

    Google’s announcement ties AI Overviews and AI Mode responses to recent Search contexts, meaning that contextual data from Search can be shared to AIO and AI Mode:.

    “You’ll also start seeing more personally relevant responses in AI Overviews and AI Mode, tailored to your recent search context.”.

    And in another passage Google explains that the contextual data from the Gemini App can be shared with AI Mode in Search:.

    “In the coming weeks you can easily share context across the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search.”.

    “So if you explore an idea in the Gemini app, AI Mode will have that foundation to build on, and vice versa.”.

    So it looks like the context data flows from Search to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as from the Gemini App to AI Mode in Search.

    The announcement identifies six connected apps:.

    According to recent reports, but Personal Intelligence is about a whole lot more. It’s about the transformation of disparate services and products into what Google CEO, Sundar Pichai, described in October 2026 as one unified search experience that’s mediated by an agentic layer.

    “I expect our agents to provide that unifying experience across these products. In fact, that agentic layer, rather than try to converge or think about different products and how they come together, I think the agentic layer naturally ends up doing that, right?

    Industry observers note that because your agents, they’re running in the cloud, they’re running 24/7, they have your context. And so they can pick up things where you left off.

    Recent findings suggest that so you can start a task in some place. You go to the other place. Your agent has that context for you.

    So I think the agentic layer offers us a chance to bring a unified product experience better than ever before.”.

    Google’s Personal Intelligence was first announced as a paid Gemini App beta feature in January 2026, which was expanded to AI Mode in search about a week later, initially supporting Gmail and Google Photos as an opt-in Search Labs experiment.

    In March it was expanded to free tier customers in the United States and within a few months it was available in 200 countries and 98 languages.

    Google unveiled the expansion of the range of information AI Mode can draw on through Personal Intelligence so that now it includes Google Wallet data, files stored in Google Drive, and Gemini conversations. Google also announced increased personalization of AI Overviews and AI Mode based on recent search activity.

    Sources indicate that opt-in connectivity of Google Wallet to AI Mode is beginning to roll out. This is really significant and ties into Sundar Pichai’s vision of Search becoming increasingly focused on helping users accomplish tasks. Google Wallet aggregates data from linked accounts like Gmail and partner apps.

    It has been revealed that google Wallet affects travel (like airline tickets), finance, commerce, event tickets, plus sensitive data (in some regions) like drivers license, and health insurance cards. When this feature is enabled, Google Wallet automatically scans incoming emails to import boarding passes, event tickets, loyalty cards, and shipping updates.

    Now all of that is connected with Personal Intelligence.

    In a recent development, connectivity to AI Mode is coming in the next few weeks. Google unveiled that connecting Google Drive to Personal Intelligence will enable AI Mode to pull information from across stored Google Drive documents, spreadsheets, and PDFs to provide personalized responses and assist users with projects, planning, and decision-making.

    “With Google Drive connected in Personal Intelligence, you can get uniquely helpful responses that take all of that context into account and help you get started, like a personalized preparation initiative ahead of tax season.”.

    Recent findings suggest that personal Intelligence will be sharing Gemini conversational context between the Gemini app and AI Mode within the next few weeks. Search personalization will come in the form of more personally relevant responses based on recent search activity.

    Personalization transparency is coming soon. Consumers will be able to see what personal context AI Mode used to generate a response and correct that information.

    Transformation Of Google Search Personal Intelligence represents a fundamental change in how Google Search (and/or AI Mode in Search) can respond to owners, incorporating knowledge about their activities alongside information from the web.

    Unification Of Google’s Products And Services Previously disparate Google products and services are now increasingly part of a unified, personalized search experience.

    Google’s Agentic Layer The expansion of Personal Intelligence is consistent with Sundar Pichai’s vision of a unified, task-based experience that maintains context across Google’s products.

    Sharing Of Contextual Data The sharing of personal and conversational context across Google’s products enables people to continue activities without having to start over.

    Expansion Beyond Information Discovery The integration of additional data sources enables Google to become increasingly useful for planning, decision-making, and accomplishing tasks.

    Increasingly Personalized Search Experiences Search responses are becoming more specific to individual customers, a change that SEOs need to really think about and integrate into how what they do fits into this newly introduced multi-dimensional level of Search.

    How To Opt Out Of Google Personal Intelligence Google is giving consumers greater insight into and control over the personal context used to generate AI Mode responses. Users can opt out or in from Personal Intelligence here.

    Google Search is increasingly an experience that’s as much about what Google knows about the user and what they want to accomplish as it is about what the user is searching for. This is arguably one of the most consequential moments in SEO that I have experienced in my nearly 30 years of experience in SEO.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that you get a thumbnail.
    • That’s right: YouTube has, at long, long last, finally allowed all creators to assign customized thumbnails to their Shorts.
    • According to recent reports, when YouTube introduced Shorts in 2020, they were its attempt to keep up with TikTok.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that you get a thumbnail. And you get a thumbnail! And you . . .

    That’s right: YouTube has, at long, long last, finally allowed all creators to assign customized thumbnails to their Shorts.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    According to recent reports, when YouTube introduced Shorts in 2020, they were its attempt to keep up with TikTok. TikTok didn’t offer custom thumbnails, because its whole platform is based on endless scrolling. The thought process was that if short-form videos did have thumbnails, people wouldn’t really see them, because videos are discovered by swiping up, not by visiting a creator’s profile.

    Recent findings suggest that but we all know that viewers do visit creators’ profiles. Not only do thumbnails–for long- or short-form–help a creator define their visual style and personal brand, but unique thumbnails help repeat viewers identify videos they’ve watched (and also, as a bonus plus, keep creators from being stuck with a perhaps unflattering moment as their content’s hero image).

    Industry observers note that tikTok later caved and added thumbnails to short-form videos. But YouTube, Land of Thumbnails, did not–at least, not until this past summer.

    In July, YouTube introduced custom Shorts thumbnails for everyone in the YouTube Partner Program, with YouTube CEO Neal Mohan saying custom thumbnails were “one of the most requested features” for the platform.

    You loved custom Shorts thumbnails—now every creator can use them on desktop and mobile!

    ✏️ Tap the pencil icon on any Short in @YouTube Studio to upload yours.

    — Neal Mohan (@nealmohan) November 23, 2026.

    YouTube’s thumbnail selection tool allowed creators to add their own images, just like with long-form videos, but also offers a TikTok-esque option where it’ll select a few screenshots from within the video and offer them as default thumbnails, for anyone who doesn’t want to apply YouTube-effort editing to their short-form content.

    Recent findings suggest that there’s one crucial thing to note from the July announcement, though: Shorts thumbnails went out to all YouTube Partner Program creators. Not to everyone–including any creators who are trying to drum up enough viewership to become a Partner creator.

    This is a significant flip from 2024, when YouTube outright noted it didn’t think Shorts thumbnails could be as impactful as long-form thumbnails. And, look, we get it: Shorts thumbnails vs long-form thumbnails is sort of like putting a half-page up against a full spread, to put things in publication terms. Shorts thumbnails inherently offer less room to work with, and thus less room to communicate videos’ vibes.

    But half-pages are still notable in the grand scheme, and considering how much watch time Shorts drives for YouTube and for creators, they should have the same audience engagement and brand identity tools as long-form content.

    Latest Update: On OnlyFans, one-time transactions are winning out over subscriptions

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (475 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Back in August, OnlyFans revealed that 5,076 creators have brought in at least $1 million each since the NSFW hub kicked off in 2016, with total creator payouts adding up to $30 billion.
    • That last figure represents a solid increase in how much creators are making on OnlyFans—but the way they’re making money on the platform has evolved in recent years, too.
    • Sources indicate that according to a recent report from Giggster, the vast majority of the $6.2 billion paid to OnlyFans creators in 2025 stemmed from non-subscription-based transactions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Back in August, OnlyFans revealed that 5,076 creators have brought in at least $1 million each since the NSFW hub kicked off in 2016, with total creator payouts adding up to $30 billion. About 20% of that $30 billion—roughly $6.2 billion—was delivered to creators during the year that ended on November 30, 2025.

    That last figure represents a solid increase in how much creators are making on OnlyFans—but the way they’re making money on the platform has evolved in recent years, too.

    Sources indicate that according to a recent report from Giggster, the vast majority of the $6.2 billion paid to OnlyFans creators in 2025 stemmed from non-subscription-based transactions. To compile its report (titled “Behind the OnlyFans Paycheck: Creator Payments, Platform Fees and U.S. Rankings”), the online marketplace combined “illustrative payment calculations with third-party estimates of OnlyFans creator accounts across all 50 states and Washington, D.C.” and examined “company-level revenue by payment type and revenue attributed to the U.S.”.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Overall, the report estimated that 700,000 OnlyFans creator accounts are active in the U.S., a number that makes up roughly 28% of the platform’s global total. And despite representing less than 30% of OnlyFans accounts, Giggster found that ~62% of OnlyFans’ platform revenue ($965.4 million) was attributed to the U.S. in the 2025 fiscal year.

    It has been revealed that one of the report’s most significant findings, however, relates to the rising importance of non-subscription-based revenue—aka payments from one-time transactions like tips, paywalled posts, paid direct messages, and custom content requests. According to Giggster, those payments generated 73% of OnlyFans’ platform revenue in the 2025 fiscal year (up from roughly 40% in 2020 and 60% in 2024).

    In a recent development, onlyFans isn’t the only creator-driven platform leaning into one-time payments, either. In a 2024 end-of-year post, Patreon noted that creators on its platform “increased monthly revenue of one-time purchases by 4x” year-over-year. More recently, a study from Ipsos commissioned by TikTok predicted that over 60,000 U.S.-based TikTok LIVE creators would make “more than the median part-time monthly income” from gift earnings in 2025.

    Recent findings suggest that youTube has devoted significant resources to one-time transactions, too. In a January blog post, CEO Neal Mohan reassured creators that the video platform would “continue to invest” in “fan funding features like Jewels and gifts,” adding that “we know these are notable revenue streams, especially outside the U.S., for creators like Santiago Matias, who uses Super Chat as a way for fans to influence the outcome of his hit reality series.”.

    At the end of the day, the rising importance of one-time transactions demonstrates an crucial truth for creators: if you want to earn more revenue, give fans more ways to pay you.

    #158657. Bing’s AI Cites Support Pages, PDFs & Staff Bios – 883,313 Citations Analyzed via @sejournal, @dodgejd

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2821 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Bing’s AI Cites Support Pages, PDFs & Staff Bios – 883,313 Citations Analyzed via @sejournal, @dodgejd

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In February, Bing launched the public preview of its AI Performance Reporting function inside Webmaster Tools.
    • Industry observers note that blog posts, product pages, and homepages account for less than half of the citations in our sample, 42% combined.
    • According to recent reports, the single most cited URL in our data set was an app page for a consumer product with an integrated mobile app component.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In February, Bing launched the public preview of its AI Performance Reporting function inside Webmaster Tools. Since then, we have been using it to gauge a bit more insight into what Bing is citing and what might be impacting those results. Monitoring different sites since then, we set out to analyze more than 883,000 AI citations across 26 brands, which surfaced a few things that may surprise you.

    Industry observers note that blog posts, product pages, and homepages account for less than half of the citations in our sample, 42% combined. The other 58% is a mix of app pages, attractions lists, instruction manuals, course catalogs, key personnel directors, and PDFs that nobody on a content team was likely thinking about.

    According to recent reports, the single most cited URL in our data set was an app page for a consumer product with an integrated mobile app component. The second was an attractions list for a tourism destination organization.

    There certainly are other tools out there at the disposal of SEOs that help us understand what AI citations might look like, but at the time, this data was reported out of the only first-party tool inside of a search engine to do so. As soon as access was provided in February, we pulled AI reports for 15 different brands and published our findings. Since then, Microsoft has added query-to-page mapping, intent and topic labels, Citation Share, and a Topics Portfolio beta. They have also backfilled much of the underlying data from previous months’ releases, allowing us to pull data for the same 15 brands, plus an additional batch to spot any gaps or trends.

    Understanding semantic differences between searchers and the fact that all of the data inside the AI Reporting is sampled to some extent, we started with the page-level reporting instead of queries. Across most sites, the pages export will provide you with a broader data set to work from, also moving you past the common practitioner question, which is “what are people prompting,” when we set out to try and better understand “what on my site does the machine actually use?”.

    We explored the AI reports from 26 different brands across nine verticals. Included were destination marketing organizations, resorts and hoteliers, ecommerce brands, B2B manufacturers, colleges and universities, an EdTech platform, regional healthcare providers, government-adjacent business services, and a financial institution.

    In a recent development, inside the AI Reporting portion, we exported the three report views for each brand: Grounding Queries, Cited Pages, and the Daily Overview. By the numbers, our overview totals delivered over 1.1 million citations across the brands, with over 883,000 on 10,861 URLs and a grounding query export of nearly 300,000 citations across 2,797 queries.

    Grounding queries are the search phrases Microsoft’s AI generates to retrieve content, not the words users type, and Microsoft states grounding query data “represents a sample of overall citation activity.” Pulling data from the fall reveals us how much of a sample. Meaning that for every brand we reviewed, the query export sums to between 5% and 39% of the overview total, and the page export is between 63% and 100%. That is why we used page counts rather than queries for pattern spotting.

    Sources indicate that two additional rules were held in the course of our analysis. First, no raw-count comparisons were used across the periods. Knowing Microsoft backfilled AI Performance data from June 1, 2026, Krishna Madhavan described the resulting jumps as “just regular data backfilling” on X. Second, the two data pulls cover different seasons, and we only carried forward the findings that held up across both, spring and fall, and set aside the ones that seasonality could explain.

    See also: Microsoft Clarity Now Demonstrates Grounding Queries Behind AI Citations.

    Across all 883,313 page citations, grouped by what the page is for:.

    According to recent reports, as one might expect, pooled numbers are leaning toward major sites, and the median brand across the data looks quite different. Product and service pages accounted for 32%, whereas editorial content was 15%, homepage 8%, and everything else thereafter was much smaller.

    Citations appear to be fairly concentrated. Across the whole set, just over 2% of the URLs carry half of all citations. Breaking this down even more, we noted that it takes 1,441 URLs in our data to reach 80%. For a typical brand, the top page alone accounts for 12.7% of its citations and takes about 40 pages to reach 80% citation volume. As conversational search continues to grow, SEOs understand that the long-tail queries are expanding, but most of what Bing’s AI pulls from is a handful of pages.

    Across destination marketing organization websites, events and things-to-do pages remain nearly 50% of the citations, and listing directories make up another 15%, with lodging-related pages falling in at under 1%. The single biggest anomaly that stood out was a tourism attraction list with nearly 17,000 citations. Grounding queries are highly seasonal, with major events and festivals delivering a large share of the citations. What does this mean for destination marketers? The sites are highly sought after and relied upon for things to do, see, and experience, though less likely for the actual places to stay.

    Industry observers note that wanting to explore more lodging-oriented searches, we added in additional resort and hotelier properties where heads in beds is a primary function of their business. Lodging and reservations pages account for 4.3% of citations across resorts, wherein activities-related content such as golf, ski, dining, and packages pages account for nearly 50% of the citations. While one resort was cited for instructional content around golf techniques, regional golf trips were more likely to garner the results that generate positive conversations in the boardroom. What does this mean for resorts and hoteliers? Monitoring these trends over the course of a season, be it summer or winter, allows a resort to see the activity mix that rotates with the calendar. It’s worth noting that a resort (not a hotel) is cited as a place that does something, and almost never as just a place to sleep.

    It has been revealed that no surprise to anyone developing SEO strategies for ecommerce brands, product and category pages account for 40% of the citations, with support and documentation-related pages residing at 26%, and specific app/login pages making up nearly 20% of the citations. Stripping out the one brand whose app page is the most cited URL in our study, the product pages rise to 64% of the citations. A second brand that pairs a physical product with an app and a service blueprint highlights the same shape. Its service plan and product support pages are two of its top three cited URLs, and PDF instruction manuals sit in its top 10. For brands that are focused on the growth of their app-enabled products, this means reviewing how you are positioned to own the support conversation. Similar to traditional search, AI models appear to be just fine citing your PDF documents, which leads to a poor customer experience and puts you down a path of hard-to-revision legacy content.

    The closer a B2B brand is to the solution being delivered, the better. Across the brands reviewed, editorial content accounted for 46% of the citations. At one manufacturing services brand with a global presence, over 70% of the citations were URLs from technical how-to articles. The same can be stated for training and tutorial-based content, especially video libraries, which accounted for 73% of citations. The exception to that is a product manufacturer whose catalog pages account for over 70% of the citations and another 10% for product literature PDFs. Meaning, if you are in the business of making highly specialized and technical products, the machine is just as happy sourcing its answers from a PDF, though again it causes more friction on the side of the customer and content teams who have to manage legacy updates over time.

    Academic programs, admissions-related pages, and financial aid make up nearly 40% of the citations for the higher ed vertical. From there, it filters out into reference material and course handouts at 13%; support and IT-related pages also at 13%; editorial articles come in at 12%, with faculty and about pages at 11%. For colleges and universities, the bulk of the pages being cited fall into more of an information-gathering category around what courses are offered, when, and the financial implications. For those working in academia, specifically higher ed, reviewing which of your pages are being referenced the most should start to provide you with insights on what your audience is seeking. If you’re a university that’s built on research and studies, there are clear signals that optimizing who your people are is a critical step that is potentially overlooked.

    Across the verticals reviewed, three categories surfaced that no content calendar is presently accounting for, and why would it? Noting PDF documents account for over 6% of all citations in total. Within the EdTech platform we reviewed, they account for nearly 17% of citations, with course catalogs also following a similar trend. Within one university, PDFs were 11% of their citations, surfacing elements from not just the course catalog but also core requirements that students need by program. Certainly, if you’re looking to own more of the conversation around your programs and what students can expect vs. letting the AI base it off of outdated PDFs, this is a prime opportunity to take action.

    Sources indicate that at one ecommerce brand, PDFs were 10.4% of all citations, all of them instruction manuals. This serves as a reminder that if a PDF is the best document you have on a subject, it could very well be cited as the best document you have on the matter itself. For brands with products that require technical support, while revising a single PDF might seem like the approach to take, consider how many PDF documents are residing in your CMS that are outdated vs. placing the actual helpful information in an HTML format on your site.

    The homepages of many websites don’t go unnoticed in our review. Homepages are 6.8% of all citations pooled, and the homepage is the single most cited page for nine of the 26 brands reviewed. When nothing else on a site carries deeper insights about the brand, its services or products, the homepage is carrying a much higher share of the citations. It doesn’t matter the size of the brand either; that’s a signal that is worth reviewing to help you determine what the AI is thinking about your brand.

    Across healthcare, education, and EdTech, people and about pages carry between 4% and 11% of citations by vertical, and 18% at one university. When the AI answer is related to who you are as a brand or an individual, where you are located, and the key individuals who work there, these pages become critical elements when directing the LLMs. How many of these page types get published once, only to never be revisited and kept up to date?

    In a recent development, looking back to an early study we did on the insights on what Bing’s Webmaster Tools was telling us about AI Citations, we revisited 15 of the original brands to determine what shifted over the course of time. Most of what moved was seasonal, and based on that, we decided to leave those elements out. However, we did find three areas worth investigating further.

    In our original review in February, login, portal, and sign-in queries accounted for approximately 18% of all citations across the brands. In the fall window, that shrunk to just above 1%.

    Within the higher education sector, 45% of the citations originally came from login and portal queries. As we observed this shift into the fall, the same number of grounding queries had dropped to just shy of 1%. Login queries for the EdTech brand also dropped from 17% to less than 1%. And while there certainly is the seasonal argument to be made, we can look at August through October as being key times at most universities and colleges as the start of a semester. We expect institutional login lookups to increase around that time, and in fact, they did not.

    It has been revealed that product support for the ecommerce brands went the other direction, with one brand’s support and access-related content rising from 17% to 42% of its citations. Noting that fall is the peak season for the brand and that demand is trending exactly where you might expect it to be.

    Bing’s June update added intent labels to the reporting, with Navigational among them. The February login queries are exactly what that label would catch. It also would appear that Microsoft has not said it suppresses AI answers differently across intent types, and what we are describing is more of a pattern to spot and not a mechanism within the report.

    According to recent reports, for the median brand, only 37% of the citations found in our February review came from query strings that still appear in the fall export, and that is before accounting for any seasonal shifts. Across each of the brand’s top ten queries this spring, we note that approximately 56% are completely absent from the fall data pull. If your brand operates around any cyclicality where it is impacted by major events, holidays, or even seasonal activities, that explains some of the difference but not all.

    It has been revealed that across the original data pull in February, we found a handful of location-only queries. Those that included [events near me], [concerts near me], and [holiday events near me], without a destination even in the query string, were present. Revisiting the same brands this fall, we see that the near me query left the data. Noting many of the AI-generated search results are favoring sites such as Eventbrite, Ticketmaster, and similar aggregator sites. The more local and regional focused your brand is, such as a multi-location storefront, the location-based data is going to be stronger and likely in line with what you experience in traditional search.

    According to recent reports, we continue to see branded searches spread into the AI Overviews in Google, yet the data coming out of Google is still not as detailed as we would like. Within Bing, we do get a view into Citation Shares, which was added in June. This reports on the percentage of citations your site receives out of all citations shown for a grounding query, which should help you determine how much of the answer your brand actually holds.

    Citation Share is Bing’s measure of how much of an answer your site has supplied. For each grounding query, it reports what percentage of all citations shown for that query pointed to your pages. On branded queries, the sites in our analysis supplied 67% of the citations, and other sites supplied 33%. On non-branded queries, the sites supplied 25% and other sites supplied 75%. Compare this to your traditional search results and determine how much your branded searches are triggering AI-generated results.

    Non-branded searches tend to always be the opportunity in traditional search, and AI-generated results are certainly no different. The data in our most recent series of exports confirms this. On a non-branded query, three of every four citations are going to someone else.

    In a recent development, up front, know that the data is all sampled, but likely the best we have to work with at the moment. The pipeline is constantly backfilling, so an increase across a three-month time period could indicate more usage, more backfill on recent dates, or both. Right now, the recommendation is to use the data as a guide and report on what the dashboard demonstrates rather than calling it growth.

    Overall, Bing’s intent labels hold up well, though it could be argued that their topic labels do not yet. Our review demonstrated one consumer product brand filed under “Home Security Systems” for 57% of its citations. Microsoft’s June post allows that labels “may be broad” for niche domains, so initiative on re-sorting them yourself. It’s also worth noting that not every grounding query traces back to a person. Queries of seven or more words grew from 1% of citations in February to 3% this fall, and some of them are plainly monitoring tools running on a schedule. Citation counts in any tool will include machine-initiated queries, and no report separates those out currently.

    It has been revealed that while Google remains the top in regards to search volume, the data coming out of their AI insights reporting is lackluster. Bing remains one of the better sources for a site owner to gauge first-party insights on what gets cited. Just be sure you read it for what it is: a sampling of your brand’s data. Have you found Bing’s AI Performance Report to be beneficial?

Clips credit and link back to the original videos, and both original creators and clippers can earn revenue through X’s engagement-based creator rewards program (aka Original Content Rewards).

    X is also beefing up monetization options for video creators. In addition to Original Content Rewards (which replaced the platform’s Revenue Sharing program earlier this fall), X has introduced Video Kickstart Bonus, “an invite-only pilot that pays creators a bonus for posting original vertical video under three minutes with no watermarks.”.

    TikTok, of course, didn’t stay offline for very long—but that hasn’t stopped X from continuing to refine its video offerings. In February of this year, the platform rolled out a redesigned immersive player intended to make video more watchable on mobile.

    With its latest slate of video features and monetization options, X finally appears to be putting its money where its mouth is—and offering creators the tools they need to take advantage.

    Camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes. With built-in governance, auditability, and human oversight, Camunda gives enterprises the control they need to move AI from pilots to production — safely and at scale. Trusted by over 700 organizations worldwide, including 9 of top 10 US banks, Camunda helps enterprises boost operational efficiency, accelerate time-to-value, and deliver better customer experiences.Fully remote and global, we are in the middle of something bigger: transforming into an AI-first organisation, built on our own platform.     In a recent development, camunda Hub is where enterprises run Camunda at scale. From Hub they manage their clusters and tenants, decide who can do what, and roll changes out across the whole organization. We’re looking for a Senior Product Builder to own the backend and architecture that let Hub manage a whole fleet of clusters. Your first focus will be the mechanism that sends access, secret, tenant and licence changes out to every connected cluster and brings deployments, health and audit records back. From there, you’ll shape Hub’s foundations: its event model, the service boundaries and data model other teams build on, and how Hub behaves when things fail or get upgraded. The platform is your product. Your users are platform administrators, Centres of Excellence and the builders across Camunda who depend on what you create. You’ll join a fresh two-person pod in our remote-first team. You’ll have real ownership as the person who makes the call, and you’ll build AI-first, from written specs through to production. Our customers run mission-critical processes on Camunda, so your work will matter to them every day.

    Take over Hub's fleet propagation mechanism from the team building its first version, and make it work for access, secrets, tenants, licences and custom roles.

    Write short design documents for foundational changes, get them reviewed by the teams that depend on them, and turn them into tested, shipped code.

    Design how Hub behaves when things go wrong: offline clusters, partial failures, Hub outages, and clusters being adopted or detached.

    Build the path from clusters back to Hub, starting with deployment inventory, health, audit records and licence status.

    Design Hub's first event and webhook mechanism, so admins and agents can react to changes instead of polling for them.

    Join the pod's rotations and Hub on-call, and help other builders take on backend work through reviews, guidelines and contract tests.

    Comfort taking a problem nobody owns yet and turning it into a design, a initiative and shipped code.

    Product judgment for technical users: you talk to the people who use your APIs and make trade-offs on their behalf.

    Press Forward gave $20 million to 205 local newsrooms over two years. Here’s how some of them spent it.

    ⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • In a recent development, we will never sell your address.
    • According to recent reports, we have sent a confirmation link to .
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    In a recent development, we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    According to recent reports, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try latest things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.

    According to recent reports, most local newsrooms in the U.S. have one thing in common: They need more money, and many dream of dollars they can use however they want.

    Recent findings suggest that RELATED ARTICLEPress Forward awards $20 million to 205 small local newsroomsSophie CulpepperOctober 16, 2024In 2024, Press Forward, the nonprofit trying to mobilize a philanthropic army for local news, announced it would give at least 100 small local newsrooms — those with annual budgets under $1 million — just that type of unrestricted funding. Almost 1,000 newsrooms applied. Ultimately, Press Forward distributed $20 million to 205 outlets. Most of them received $100,000 each, split over two years.

    I wondered what the recipients had done with the money, and which problems it had (or hadn’t) solved. Between May and October, I spoke or emailed with more than 30 grantees.

    The grantees represented every U.S. state, came from cities, suburbs, and rural areas, and published in multiple languages. They included for-profits and nonprofits, print and digital-only publications, college newsrooms, and public radio stations. Statewide newsrooms with fully staffed teams like The Maine Monitor, scrappy news startups like 285 South, and community newspapers powered by freelancers and part-time staff like the Copper River Record in Alaska all received funding.

    According to recent reports, for many newsrooms, Press Forward was the first grant they’d ever applied for. “Many of the country’s newsrooms are small, and few get foundation grants,” stated Press Forward executive director Dale Anglin. The open call was designed to change that and to distribute the money swiftly. Grantees were required to complete two LION sustainability audits a year apart; Press Forward is analyzing that data now and will release its findings next month.1.

    RELATED ARTICLEA study of nonprofit newsrooms reveals some cracks in the model’s foundationSeth C. LewisOctober 6, 2026“People tell me that what Press Forward did was unusual and rare within philanthropy,” said María José Ramírez Braiz, founder and CEO of Midwest-based grantee Te Lo Cuento News.

    “They remarked to us at the beginning of the grant period, before the shit hit the fan with the federal government, ‘If you need this money to keep the lights on, keep the lights on,'” said Copper River Record editor Allison Sayer, one of the paper’s two part-time staffers. “I feel that this was really a gift.”.

    First-time grant applicants and recipients, in particular, mentioned Press Forward’s recognition gave them credibility and visibility with other funders. And publishers described the funding as a morale boost that validated low-paid work.

    Sources indicate that “It has been a life-changer, a lifesaver for us,” stated Gretchen Sporleder Orr, who publishes the World Journal in southern Colorado with her husband. Her voice broke when she talked to me about the funding. “I don’t know if we would be in business right now if it wasn’t for the Press Forward money.”.

    The Real WV “would not still exist without Press Forward,” mentioned Stephen Baldwin, the site’s volunteer publisher. (He’s also the former minority leader for the West Virginia Senate and a pastor of two churches.) The outlet was one of eight grantees that received just two $25,000 grants over two years. “There’s not exactly a lot of capital floating around West Virginia for nonprofit news,” Baldwin said, “and without this outside impact, we wouldn’t be able to do this work.” But he hopes that the site can be less reliant on grants in the future.

    The funding did not save every recipient. One grantee, Atlanta Civic Circle, shut down earlier this year. Atlanta Civic Circle did not receive its second $50,000 grant because it didn’t complete the first LION audit, Anglin stated. (Atlanta Civic Circle did not respond to my request for an interview, but executive director Saba Long wrote on LinkedIn in June that “the funding environment for local nonprofit journalism is extraordinarily difficult right now.”) Other recipients have merged or transformed since applying for the grant.2.

    Recent findings suggest that RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026Medill’s annual State of Local News report, released this month, describes a local news ecosystem in a “state of precarity.” That state of precariousness helps explain how $100,000 over two years can be a “godsend,” a “miracle,” and not enough. As one grantee put it, “Right now, these are shanties built on a beach, waiting for a hurricane to come through.”.

    Sources indicate that “Press Forward reached newsrooms that don’t have existing relationships with major national funders,” remarked Nina Ignaczak, the founder, publisher, and editor of Planet Detroit. “The challenge now is whether the commitment holds.”.

    The funding helped newsrooms keep the lights on, whether they used it to pay bills, pay down debt, make payroll, or as a buffer when something went wrong.

    “The flexibility that Press Forward has given us has allowed us to fill — I wouldn’t say emergencies, but unexpected gaps,” noted Richard Young, founder and executive director of CivicLex in Kentucky. It brought on a consulting editor to keep city hall coverage going after losing a reporter, and purchased fresh software. Without the funding, CivicLex likely would have had to dip into its reserves, he said.

    Bob Bonnar, publisher of the News Letter Journal in Wyoming, used the first payment from Press Forward to upgrade computers and cameras and give some staffers raises. “That chewed up the money very rapidly,” he said, “and I probably should have held some of it back because the News Letter Journal ended up having a pretty rough year in 2025.” He had to use about half of the second $50,000 payment to repay an operating loan. The rest covered the remaining revenue shortfall and kept the organization in the black through the winter.

    Vandana Kumar, publisher of the California-based ethnic media outlet India Currents, described the funding as a “stabilizing force” that allowed the newsroom to keep operating despite a contraction in philanthropic giving and cuts to local government advertising.

    The Copper River Record built infrastructure to host digital ads and created a new website. It held listening sessions with Native villages in its coverage area and donated subscriptions to local Tribal offices. It improved the design of its print newspaper. Sayer paid freelancers to complete Press Pass training and pursued other professional development. And she was able to take on more ambitious stories about PFAS and “forever chemicals.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the Press Forward funding was “the biggest single windfall in nearly 20 years for our small community newspaper,” Sandpoint Reader publisher Ben Olson told me. The Idaho-based paper used the money to travel to the state capital for Press Club awards and design a fresh media kit, which Olson said has improved ad sales. The Reader also paid a large chunk of its printing bill, paid its rent a year in advance, and gave staffers bonuses. (The bonuses helped the paper become 100% employee-owned; Olson’s two employees bought in when Olson’s business partner and co-owner retired.).

    It has been revealed that the open-ended nature of the grants gave Colorado’s World Journal “the flexibility to be able to make a change, do a thing, and then pivot as needed,” Sporleder Orr stated. “When we were in the toilet, all I could think about was, like, ‘Is there going to be anything in the post office today so that I can make payroll?’ ‘Oh, my God, we’ve got to pay rent.’” Sometimes she and her husband skipped their own paychecks to pay staff. The grant gave them “emotional bandwidth” to strategy ahead.

    Many grantees used the funding to hire full- or part-time staffers. Sometimes, that worked out well.

    The Mānoa Mirror, an online newsroom based at the University of Hawaii at Mānoa, received two $25,000 grants, which it used to hire a managing editor, a student editorial coordinator, three student reporters, and a social media producer. (The managing editor was paid a stipend, and the other positions were part-time.) The work had previously depended on “faculty goodwill and volunteerism, which was not sustainable for long,” remarked Hye-ryeon Lee, who was professor and chair of the school of communication and information until retiring this summer. With the fresh hires, the site went from publishing a few stories a month to publishing daily.

    The Real WV’s first LION audit pointed to a need its small team had already recognized: hiring someone to sell ads. It hired a public school teacher with sales experience (including selling ads for the yearbook) part-time.

    It has been revealed that the funding allowed Te Lo Cuento News to pay contributors consistently and to add contract, part-time positions including a sales manager, an office administrator, and a couple of reporters. The only position it could sustain beyond the grant period is the part-time sales manager, Ramírez Braiz mentioned.

    The Texas Spur is one of five weekly newspapers owned by Paragraph Ranch Media. Originally, the team planned to use the Press Forward grant to secure a loan to improve manufacturer housing and hire a journalist based in Spur (population 863 as of 2020). But nobody took the newspaper up on the free housing offer, remarked editor and general manager Barbara Brannon. So the company hired four early-career journalists (two full-time, two part-time) living in its 10-county coverage area. Three of the four left for jobs in other industries halfway through their second year. The one who stayed is doing well as a regional sports reporter, Brannon said, and a hire who replaced a person who left is now managing editor for The Post Dispatch.3.

    The turnover Brannon experienced isn’t unique to Spur. Other newsrooms also found hiring with grant money challenging.

    It has been revealed that sometimes, that was because of location. “Had we been able to find the right people from the outset, I believe the grant would have had a greater impact on the business,” stated Anton Kaufer, regional publisher for Hagadone Media Montana. In rural Northwest Montana, though, recruiting and retaining staff is a challenge, and Hagadone’s Mineral Independent struggled to replace its salesperson and office manager after they retired. The experience “reinforced for us that sustainability isn’t just about having the funding,” Kaufer said. “It’s also about having the people in place to make the most of it.”.

    The World Journal tried placing an ad for a salesperson with the Colorado Press Association and got “absolutely no interest,” Sporleder Orr said. “People living in northern Colorado don’t particularly want to come live in a teeny-tiny town in a rural, broke part of the state.” (She credited the grant with giving her the mental space to fire a salesperson who wasn’t working out, then regroup.).

    It has been revealed that other times, the money just wasn’t enough. “The reality is that $100,000 over two years isn’t a lot,” one grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. “You can’t hire somebody with that.”.

    In a recent development, ecoRI’s experience illustrates those limitations. Before receiving the Press Forward grant, EcoRI had used other grant funding and reserves to hire a director of development in a one-year contract position. In its grant application to Press Forward, the team proposed converting that role into a full-time staff position with benefits.

    Sources indicate that the salary limited the hiring pool, though. The development director position paid $65,000 a year, which “is really not the market rate for a director of development” in the area, publisher and cofounder Jo Detz remarked. (She said it should be more like $90,000.) The staffer they ended up hiring came from another state and hadn’t worked in news before. In a staff position, he cost more than he was bringing in. Detz laid him off and eliminated the position last December. She called the experience “heartbreaking.”.

    “At the point where I knew this wasn’t working,” she said, “there wasn’t enough runway to pivot, rethink, rehire.”.

    In a recent development, beyond the salary limitations, Detz thinks the development director didn’t have enough runway to succeed. The kind of development the staffer was hired to oversee — major gifts and individual giving — is a long game; “that position would need at least two or three years to begin to see some benefits,” she noted. Now, she’s back where she started, juggling fundraising with her other work.

    “I know it’s crazy to say that $100,000 over two years wasn’t enough,” she remarked, “but it was not enough to make a meaningful difference to our revenue strategy.”.

    It has been revealed that planet Detroit’s Ignaczak was in a unique position: Around the same time the newsroom received the Press Forward grant, Planet Detroit also received a $500,000 three-year grant from the MacArthur Foundation. That grant allowed her to hire a managing editor, she said.

    Recent findings suggest that ignaczak believes general operating support is what small nonprofit newsrooms need. But to be effective, “I really think fully funding a revenue role for a minimum of three years is what needs to happen to build sustainability, if that is the goal,” she said. “And $100,000 over two years is not enough to achieve that.”.

    Sources indicate that notiVisión Georgia, a Spanish-language local news outlet with one full-time staffer, is committed to print in a world moving away from it. The print newspaper is the only way the outlet has been able to use to “generate real economic value,” said CEO Mónica Pirela, because it’s where local companies want to place ads. The organization spent some of its Press Forward funds on printing and distribution. Pirela wears “every hat” right now, and the organization’s top need is a dedicated sales manager, she said.

    According to recent reports, california’s BenitoLink, meanwhile, used some of the Press Forward funding to begin printing in 2025. That will allow it to apply for newspaper of record status and get paid for running legal notices.

    Industry observers note that in Minnesota, Swift County Monitor-News publisher and owner Reed Anfinson called the grant a “godsend” at a time when tariffs and rising gas prices have driven up printing and delivery costs and weakened advertisers’ budgets. The for-profit Monitor-News put some of its Press Forward funding toward redesigning its print newspaper. Anfinson also purchased materials as part of an “Out of Sight/Out of Mind” advertising campaign stressing the value of print. (He created the campaign himself, using Midjourney for the images.) For news organizations in small towns, Anfinson believes, digital revenue will never be enough to sustain operations.

    Some organizations used the funding to expand their remit beyond news.

    Sources indicate that for instance, the Copper River Record partnered with the Copper River Native Association to include weekly language graphics in the paper for Ahtna, a critically endangered language, coordinating with a local kindergarten class. That project required a lot of time and investment up front, Sayer said, but it can continue beyond the life of the grant.

    Industry observers note that planet Detroit used some Press Forward funding for reporting, but “the most significant thing the grant made possible wasn’t any single story,” Ignaczak stated. The grant gave the team time to work on its Civic Action Toolbox, which turns reporting into civic engagement prompts. In a story about a local ballot proposal, for instance, the embedded toolbox flags upcoming public meetings, links to contact information for local representatives, and suggests an organization to follow. The tool is also in beta testing with other newsrooms.

    Industry observers note that “The whole project came from having the space to ask what our readers actually need from us beyond information, and then building toward that,” Ignaczak remarked. “Unrestricted funding makes that kind of work possible.”.

    Anfinson of the Monitor-News took the unusual step of writing a grant application on behalf of the local school district, which was losing students to adjacent districts. He used some of the Press Forward funding to match a $2,500 grant to the district. The district then ran $5,000 in ads in a “goodwill effort” to stem declining enrollment. The partnership helped to raise the Monitor-News’s profile, he noted, by highlighting the benefits of newspaper advertising.

    Industry observers note that press Forward required grantees to complete two LION sustainability audits. But it also offered optional coaching via the media consulting organization Blue Engine to help implement the first audit’s recommendations. Of the 205 grantees, 154 participated in coaching, Anglin remarked.

    Industry observers note that the coaching kicked off in January, with most individual coaches and grantees meeting monthly. Multiple participants mentioned the support would have been more beneficial if it were introduced earlier. This was a tradeoff of Press Forward moving quickly to get money out the door, Anglin said.4.

    In a recent development, this was the first large, unrestricted grant Austin Common had ever received, and it struggled with how to spend the money. “It felt like a lot of pressure,” remarked Amy Stansbury, the site’s editor-in-chief and only full-time staffer.

    Stansbury wanted to bring on the organization’s first full-time employees, but didn’t want to make those hires (and spend all the grant money) until she had a clear plan. The coaching helped her figure out which hires made the most strategic sense and how to budget for them.

    A few publishers were lukewarm about the substance of the coaching, but the majority I heard from were enthusiastic. At first, Baldwin was skeptical and worried the coaching might amount to “checking a box.” In practice, though, he said it’s been “tremendously helpful” for tasks like writing the job description for the Real WV’s sales position.

    Sources indicate that sporleder Orr called the coaching “incredible.” The monthly sessions helped her with everything from tackling grant proposals to improving her Google Analytics skills. The combination of money and coaching, she added, “makes sure that the recipients don’t just continue doing business as usual.”.

    Sources indicate that in addition to the funding, Press Forward paid for grantees to attend conferences. Anglin noted 111 grantees attended the Lenfest News Philanthropy Summit in Philadelphia in 2025, 81 attended the same conference (which I also attended) in 2026, and 87 attended the Business of Local conference in Salt Lake City in 2025. A handful of grantees attended affinity conferences.

    According to recent reports, stansbury found attending conferences for the first time helpful and eye-opening. It taught her “there’s this secret shadow world of [invitation-only] foundation and grant funding.” Press Forward’s travel support to attend a national conference was “transformative” for India Currents, Kumar said, giving it visibility and access to relationship-building.

    To small newsrooms, the grant felt like a Press Forward stamp of approval that put them on the map for other funders. The Mirror’s Lee called the Press Forward funding “instrumental” in securing a $20,000 grant from a local foundation. But that was an exception among publishers I heard from; most didn’t feel the visibility and credibility conferred by the grant directly translated to other funders giving them more money.

    According to recent reports, so several publishers, including Ramírez Braiz of Te Lo Cuento News, would like to see Press Forward go a step further and make individual introductions to funders. “Those more personal introductions can make a major difference for small organizations,” she noted.

    Ramírez Braiz also called for “more shared learning around outcomes and impact.” Few grantees had a good sense of what others in the cohort were up to, and some were interested in more knowledge sharing with peer organizations, though the day-to-day grind of keeping one’s own newsroom running was a common impediment.

    Since 2023, Anglin mentioned, Press Forward’s network of more than 130 funders has invested $258 million directly in newsrooms. That suggests that over half of the more than $400 million the coalition notes it’s invested has gone to newsrooms.

    When Press Forward first unveiled the direct funding for newsrooms, it “felt really awesome,” the grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. To the grantee, it was meaningful to see Press Forward give funding to more organizations than planned in response to the scale of need. But when Press Forward went on to a second funding round in which single organizations, including both newsrooms and newsroom-adjacent organizations like the International Women’s Media Foundation and LION, received as much as $1.5 million for infrastructure projects, the same grantee said it felt like “a slap in the face.”.

    “Many of the problems newsrooms face aren’t unique to them individually,” Anglin mentioned. “If we are attempting to solve problems at scale, we have to intervene not just at the newsroom level, but at the systems level, too.” She said that because many of the infrastructure grantees serve multiple newsrooms, “investing in them creates a multiplier effect across the industry.”.

    According to recent reports, the argument that funding support organizations and infrastructure lifts more boats is “a cop-out,” this publisher remarked. “I think the philanthropists know it, I think the associations know it, and I think the potential grantees that are not funders or associations or intermediaries know it.”.

    Young had a different perspective. Because of CivicLex’s broad scope, it seeks out funding from both democracy funders and journalism funders. Young thinks local news funders are way ahead on getting dollars into local communities.

    It has been revealed that “I think Press Forward has done one of the more effective jobs of anything I’ve seen in the broader landscape of my world, and the civic renewal space, of delivering resources to the local level,” he remarked. (He added, “No one is ever happy in the local news ecosystem when I say that folks in the local news ecosystem don’t know how good they have it. That does not win me a lot of friends.”).

    Most publishers I heard from see grants like this as critical to continued operation, yet they’re wary of overreliance on philanthropy.

    Young said he’d be surprised if local news is still a focus for national philanthropy in eight years. “Filling your cup up with money that will be impossible to recover in four years is a danger zone,” he added.

    In a recent development, right now, more than 80% of Planet Detroit’s revenue mix comes from foundations. Ignaczak remarked the organization hopes to bring that down to 50% by 2028. “But for nonprofit newsrooms covering environmental and public health issues in a mid-size metro, general operating grants aren’t a crutch,” she said. “They’re infrastructure.”.

    Recent findings suggest that as for Press Forward, “Time will tell, as these grants go away, what impact [they’ve] actually had on the newsrooms that received [them], how many have managed to build sustainability,” she added. “I think a newsroom that needed $50,000 to survive to next year had problems that $50,000 isn’t going to solve.”.

    LOOKOUT executive director Jake Hylton believes there’s enough funding to go around. “While there may not be enough to support every single newsroom at a very large amount,” he noted, “I do believe that there is a larger investment in news that could be done.”.

    A second grantee who asked to stay anonymous was blunt about their fears for the future. “We’re scared shitless about 2027,” this person noted, “because not only is the Press Forward money not returning, we also see none of the national grants that sustained us in 2024 and previous years.”.

    It has been revealed that the Copper River Record was in the black before receiving this grant, and the lean paper’s fixed overhead remains low. For the Record, Press Forward has been like “a fairy godmother,” Sayer said.

    “I’m not going to lie: I will miss having the money to say yes to any reasonable story,” she continued. “But I think that, even going back to our original budget, the strength of what we learned will continue to help us deliver a higher quality paper that is more relevant to the communities we serve.”.

    Industry observers note that the Sandpoint Reader, Olson stated, is “surviving” right now. “We’d love to be thriving,” he added, “but we’re happy to continue to survive when many print publications aren’t.” He credited the Press Forward grant with giving the burned-out team “the chance to fall in love with our industry again.”.

    Sporleder Orr feels nervous about what’s ahead, but with the World Journal in a much more comfortable cash flow position, she and her husband are “in a way better mental state about the business.”.

    In a recent development, “We feel good about the future right now, that we are going to be able to keep going and make it,” she stated. “We’re back to, ‘This is what we do ’til we die.'”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As a Coalesce Sales Engineer, ideally based in Sydney or Melbourne, you will play a pivotal role in driving our sales efforts by leveraging your technical expertise and exceptional communication skills. Collaborating closely with the sales team, you will be the bridge between our technology and our clients, delivering compelling technical demonstrations and guiding customers towards successful implementations. Your ability to showcase the value and capabilities of Coalesce's offerings will be instrumental in driving growth and customer satisfaction. You will primarily cover Australia and Upcoming Zealand, working alongside Account Executives and the Partner team.

    Engage in technical discussions with prospective clients to understand their unique challenges and data requirements.

    Own technical relationship with prospects throughout the sales process. Run discovery, demos, and POCs. Lead architecture reviews.

    Develop and deliver compelling technical presentations, showcasing the capabilities and features of Coalesce's solutions.

    Collaborate with customers to understand their data ecosystem, workflows, and integration points, providing tailored solutions to address their needs.

    Craft and present technical proposals that effectively communicate the benefits of Coalesce's technology in solving complex business problems.

    Serve as the technical liaison between clients and internal teams, conveying customer feedback and contributing to product enhancement discussions.

    Stay up-to-date with industry trends, competitive landscape, and emerging technologies such as AI to effectively position Coalesce's offerings.

    Continuously build expertise in Coalesce's technical features, use cases, and integration possibilities.

    5+ years in data engineering, analytics engineering or data platform roles, including at least 2 years as a Sales Engineer, Solutions Engineer or similar technical sales role.

    Strong technical understanding of data engineering concepts, ETL processes, and data transformation methodologies.

    Experience with MCP and governing AI agents' in building and managing data infrastructure. Strong technical understanding of agentic AI and how it is used in data engineering.

    Familiarity with data governance and data observability concepts and their relationship with data engineering.

    Proficiency in SQL and demonstrated experience working with Snowflake and the Snowflake partner ecosystem, or other cloud data platform such as Databricks or Google BigQuery.

    Excellent communication skills, with the ability to convey complex technical concepts to both technical and non-technical audiences.

    Demonstrated problem-solving skills and a consultative approach to understanding and addressing customer challenges.

    Self-motivated, proactive, and results-driven mindset with a focus on driving customer success.

    Willingness to travel as needed to support customer engagements and attend industry events.

    Experience with version control systems (e.g., Git) and collaborative development practices.

    Bachelor's degree in a technical field, such as Computer Science, Engineering, or related disciplines (or equivalent practical experience).

    Competitive salary and performance-based incentives.

    Contribution toward private health insurance.

    Employer superannuation contributions in line with the Superannuation Guarantee.

    Flexible work arrangements and remote work options.

    Professional development opportunities and continuous learning.

    Collaborative and innovative work environment.

    If you are a passionate technologist with a strong background in data engineering, a proven ability to drive technical sales, and a desire to contribute to transformative solutions, we invite you to apply. Join us in shaping the future of data transformation and analytics at Coalesce.

    Recent findings suggest that since our founding in 2020, Coalesce has been on a mission to improve the lives of data professionals by making data transformation as efficient and intuitive as possible. We’re putting an end to the days of arduous manual coding and inflexible GUIs by providing a best of both worlds solution.

    In a recent development, we're a remote and culture-first manufacturer. We believe that a strong, intentional culture is key to attracting and retaining world-class talent. Here, you’ll find a workplace built on radical honesty, deep trust, empathy, and a shared commitment to continuous learning and growth.

    Coalesce is an equal opportunity employer. We welcome applicants of all backgrounds and are committed to fostering an inclusive, accessible environment. If you need accommodations during the application process, please let us know.

    Recent findings suggest that need another reason to read that 47,212th article about paywall strategy? What if it earned you a point?

    According to recent reports, for decades now, news publishers have been yammering on about “gamifying” the news. But what about gamifying the news about the news?

    Welcome to the Nieman Lab News-About-News Quiz, a weekly incentive to keep up with the latest happenings in the world of digital journalism. All questions will be based on the week’s Nieman Lab stories or articles elsewhere that we’ve linked to in What We’re Reading. (And unlike other ways of gamifying news events, we promise not to bankrupt anybody.).

    The quiz will appear here for the next four Fridays as a trial run; if people seem to like it, we’ll keep it going in 2027. Good luck!

    Google Confirms November 2026 Core Patch Is Complete via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (633 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google’s November 2026 core revision finished rolling out on Nov.
    • The dashboard’s latest entry, posted at 6:03 a.m.
    • Sources indicate that glenn Gabe, SEO and AI Search Consultant at G-Squared Interactive, dates the revision’s impact to Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google’s November 2026 core revision finished rolling out on Nov. 24, according to the Search Status Dashboard, putting the first post-update week Google suggests comparing in Search Console on U.S. Thanksgiving, Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

    The dashboard’s latest entry, posted at 6:03 a.m. PT, reads: “The rollout was complete as of November 24, 2026.” The enhancement began rolling out Nov. 10, so it finished inside the two-week window Google gave at launch, which I covered that day.

    Sources indicate that glenn Gabe, SEO and AI Search Consultant at G-Squared Interactive, dates the revision’s impact to Nov. 13, three days after the rollout began. In a Nov. 17 post on X, he wrote that he believed the update “landed on Friday the 13th,” with Search Console showing massive surges and drops for affected sites starting that day.

    Gabe leaned on Search Console because third-party SEO tools were “all over the place due to poisoning, filtering, etc.” By Nov. 20, he remarked the tools’ trend lines matched what he saw in Search Console for those sites.

    Lily Ray, Founder of Algorythmic and VP, SEO & AI Search at Amsive, shared a chart on LinkedIn on Nov. 23 showing subfolders and subdomains on six sites that “have been dropping fast since Google’s November core upgrade started.” Each folder held one template repeated thousands of times, such as a page per word, per area code or per “X vs Y” word pairing. She wrote that most of the folders target searches “not closely related to the business offering.”.

    Ray wrote that within each site, “the content section (blog, resources, etc.) is falling hard while the main product/brand pages stay strong.” She has seen AI Overview and AI Mode citations to those folders “show similar drops” too. Her chart uses SISTRIX visibility data, with the same trend lines checked in Ahrefs, and doesn’t name the sites.

    It has been revealed that ray called these “latest examples of the exact same SEO challenges that have been hurting sites during core updates for years.” In an Oct. 7 column for SEJ, she listed templated, programmatic pages among the patterns she’d found on sites hit by Google updates this year.

    Google’s recommendations for core updates suggest waiting until at least a full week after an upgrade has finished rolling out, then trying to compare a week of data post-rollout, Nov. 25 to Dec. 1 on this update’s dates, to a week of data pre-rollout such as Nov. 3-9.

    It has been revealed that for retail sites, the week prior to the rollout will include regular traffic while the week immediately following the rollout includes Black Friday and may reflect holiday traffic. Another check would be comparing the same holiday traffic from last year alongside Google’s suggested comparative week.

    Marie Haynes wrote for SEJ that the click spike some site owners were seeing in their Search Console from Oct. 31-Nov. 2 wasn’t human traffic. A baseline start date of Nov. 3 excludes those days. There is also a logging issue listed on Google’s data anomalies page that resulted in lower impression counts in the Generative AI performance report for Nov. 9-11, which coincides with the end of the baseline week.

    Using a page path filter in the Performance report allows you to isolate your product pages and compare these to a templated content folder as described by Ray. Google’s guidance also indicates to avoid making changes to content that’s already performing well.

    In a recent development, the first full week after completion ends Dec. 1, so the comparison Google suggests can run once that day’s data reaches Search Console. Gabe wrote on Nov. 20 that tremors and reversals “can always happen as Google updates additional core systems” or spots something off in its results after an update.
