    Everyone wants a piece of creator IPs. Outshine Talent founder Barbara Jones is making that work in her clients’ favor.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (974 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Creator IPs have been the talk of the town this year, and we don’t expect that to change as we head into 2027.
    • While much of the attention around this new media “gold rush” has focused on mainstream entertainment companies (finally) recognizing creators’ value, we think it’s equally as key to spotlight development efforts happening within established creator-space companies.
    • Sources indicate that that’s why we chatted with Barbara Jones, who founded Outshine Talent in 2019.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Creator IPs have been the talk of the town this year, and we don’t expect that to change as we head into 2027. As you’ll know if you’re a regular Tubefilter reader, there are many creator IP projects in the works–some with major Hollywood studios, some with Netflix and Disney, some with smaller independent studios, and some produced entirely by creators themselves (maybe with a little help from YouTube?).

    While much of the attention around this new media “gold rush” has focused on mainstream entertainment companies (finally) recognizing creators’ value, we think it’s equally as key to spotlight development efforts happening within established creator-space companies.

    Sources indicate that that’s why we chatted with Barbara Jones, who founded Outshine Talent in 2019. Prior to launching Outshine, Jones founded influencer marketing agency Intuition Media Group, where she spent 12 years, and also served as a founding board member of the Influencer Marketing Association.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Industry observers note that jones recently expanded Outshine to a newly introduced arm, called Outshine Entertainment, that focuses on helping creators build original IPs across things like short films, microdramas, full-length films, and TV; it also produces live events. Outshine is encouraging its clients to take creative chances and make their dream projects, and is also encouraging studios and streamers that could offer financial and production support for those projects to get involved.

    Some of Outshine Entertainment’s current and prospective creator projects include:.

    Recent findings suggest that “It’s a natural evolution for a lot of these creators to say, ‘I want to do more,'” Jones notes. “‘I’m a great writer, I’m a comedian, I’m an actor, I want to do more of these things.’ And I feel the industry is actually realizing the value and saying, ‘Yeah, I think you’re right. We need to start supporting these newly introduced, fresh faces, fresh ideas, things that are maybe a little more inexpensive and worth taking a shot on, seeing what we can do.'”.

    Sources indicate that jones says she feels the atmosphere right now is ripe for creators to experiment, and to license out their production ideas to places like Tubi that are willing to take the ride with them. She believes creators keeping a relatively low production cost will spur companies to support them.

    It has been revealed that “We’re filling the pipeline with originals and upcoming ideas and things that don’t have to cost a fortune to try and test,” she notes. “Creators have that ability to test things out, see where they go, and then expand upon them if something’s really, really going.”.

    She points to the Romano Brothers series as an example. Sahid, Maystrik, and Hernandez originally created the series as a parody of popular love sibling-rivalry love triangles in reveals like The Summer I Turned Pretty. They weren’t sure it would take off, but they threw it up on TikTok–and after a very enthusiastic reception from viewers, they committed to the idea and turned it into a full-fledged original series with Tubi.

    According to recent reports, successful creators tend to be inherently good at identifying what content resonates with their viewers, and how to build on that content’s themes and ideas to widen the scope and keep people coming back. That’s exactly what happened with Never Have I Ever Spent the Winter with the Romano Brothers.

    It has been revealed that “They had just done it for themselves,” Jones says. “But they realized it would turn into something because it had audience interest. And that’s the fun part about it. I always say to our talent: The gatekeepers are gone. You’ve just got to try it. Just make it. We can always find money. We can find resources. We can find those things, but everyone’s looking for fresh ideas, for ingenuity.”.

    She points to another plus of working with creators: They’re “speedboats” whereas traditional entertainment tends to be a “cruise ship.”.

    According to recent reports, with creators, “You can be quicker to try things,” she says. “And, for the first time, I’m really feeling like there are outside forces that want to help creators fund some of these things.”.

    With that funding in hand, creators are “leveling up, because now these are productions versus being solo, making everything yourself,” Jones states.

    Industry observers note that some funding can come from brands, Jones thinks. “I was just talking to a brand at one of our events, and I was saying, Why aren’t we just doing a microdrama? Let’s just do a microdrama that has product placement in it, but is actually a fun storyline,” she states. “That takes a normal sponsored post to the next level. We have to start thinking differently. I really believe creators are modern media, and I think people are catching up to that and realizing [a creator’s] audience is what they need to be focused on.”.

    We’ve already seen a few brands push in and build their own microdramas to advertise products. It’s not far-fetched at all to envision a world where Sahid, Maystrik, and Hernandez’s next parody project comes with a sponsor–maybe even one that’s willing to be a little self-aware and play along with the satire. Imagine a classic romcom “oh no, there’s only one bed and it’s snowing outside so we have to cuddle!” situation sponsored by a cozy sleepwear manufacturer, or a hot cocoa brand.

    Jones notes supporting creators’ original IPs is a top priority for Outshine going into 2027.

    “It’s very exciting. I have a lot of young, fresh faces who are super creative and love to have ideas, and now I feel like I actually have places to bring them,” she says. “I have people who are really listening to what creators can do.”.

    #158645. Tech Report: Elon Musk’s Grokipedia is littered with mistakes. But Wikipedia could still learn some things from it.

    📅 02 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 26m • 📚 Deep Dive (5132 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Elon Musk’s Grokipedia is littered with mistakes. But Wikipedia could still learn some things from it.

    📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5132 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • We have sent a confirmation link to .
    • Grokipedia highlights that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Grokipedia highlights that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.

    In a recent development, when I saw Grokipedia’s articles about me, the memories came rushing back: my 19 years in minor league baseball, including that impressive season with the Montgomery Rebels when I hit 20 home runs. I was lean back then — 6 feet tall and 168 pounds — and earned a career batting average just under .300. I became a minor league coach and managed the Chicago White Sox for a short stint in 1970, which Grokipedia stated “highlighted [my] readiness for higher-level responsibilities.”.

    I then attended Arizona State University, switched to a career in journalism, created the fact-checking site PolitiFact, won a Pulitzer Prize, and now teach journalism at Duke University.

    Sources indicate that ah, the memories!…except that I never played minor league baseball, never managed the White Sox, and can only dream about being 6 feet tall. (I’m 5’8″.) Grokipedia, the AI-written encyclopedia of Elon Musk, has confused me with Marion Danne “Bill” Adair, who died in 2002.

    Industry observers note that that article and another one about “Bill Adair (journalist)” — which really is me — illustrate the many flaws of Grokipedia, which introduced a year ago. The articles are littered with mistakes and superfluous details. They are terribly written and ridiculously long. If Grok, the AI engine that wrote this turgid prose, were a student in one of my writing courses, I would give it a D. (Editor’s note: After this article was published, someone updated the inaccurate Grok pages. The original versions are linked here.).

    In a recent development, still, the articles provide valuable lessons for Wikipedia editors who are debating how and when to use AI. Grokipedia adds new content and context that Wikipedia often lacks. It shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet and summarizing them in sweeping prose. It can also provide balance to articles that need it.

    Grok can’t write worth a lick, but it reveals how Wikipedia can take advantage of AI at a time when overworked editors are trying to keep the encyclopedia alive.

    Recent findings suggest that musk debuted Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he said was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet. With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a latest version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.” When Grokipedia launched, Musk said he had big aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video. Maybe someday. For now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia demonstrates edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make. Last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk. Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites. Wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.) By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder. Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times. Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models. In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race. Five other errors showed Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok said I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor. The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too rapidly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a big scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.” I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop. Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s important and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important. The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.” Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty. Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR. My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles. After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities. Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

    Industry observers note that musk launched Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he remarked was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet.

    With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a upcoming version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.”.

    Industry observers note that when Grokipedia introduced, Musk stated he had major aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video.

    Industry observers note that for now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia shows edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make.

    Sources indicate that last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk.

    According to recent reports, grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites. Wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.) By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder. Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times. Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models. In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race. Five other errors indicated Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok said I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor. The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too promptly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a major scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.” I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop. Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s vital and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important. The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.” Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty.     Engage in technical discussions with prospective clients to understand their unique challenges and data requirements.

    Develop and deliver compelling technical presentations, showcasing the capabilities and features of Coalesce's solutions.

    Collaborate with customers to understand their data ecosystem, workflows, and integration points, providing tailored solutions to address their needs.

    Craft and present technical proposals that effectively communicate the benefits of Coalesce's technology in solving complex business problems.

    Serve as the technical liaison between clients and internal teams, conveying customer feedback and contributing to product enhancement discussions.

    Stay up-to-date with industry trends, competitive landscape, and emerging technologies to effectively position Coalesce's offerings.

    Continuously build expertise in Coalesce's technical features, use cases, and integration possibilities.

    Bachelor's degree in a technical field, such as Computer Science, Engineering, or related disciplines (or equivalent practical experience).

    Proven track record as a Sales Engineer, Solutions Engineer, or similar technical sales role.

    Strong technical understanding of data engineering concepts, ETL processes, and data transformation methodologies.

    Strong technical understanding of agentic AI and how it is used in data engineering.

    Proficiency in SQL and demonstrated experience working with Snowflake and the Snowflake partner ecosystem, or other cloud data platform such as Databricks or Google Major Query.

    Excellent communication skills, with the ability to convey complex technical concepts to both technical and non-technical audiences.

    Demonstrated problem-solving skills and a consultative approach to understanding and addressing customer challenges.

    Experience with version control systems (e.g., Git) and collaborative development practices.

    Self-motivated, proactive, and results-driven mindset with a focus on driving customer success.

    Willingness to travel as needed to support customer engagements and attend industry events.

    Competitive salary and performance-based incentives.

    Contribution toward private health insurance.

    Employer superannuation contributions in line with the Superannuation Guarantee.

    Flexible work arrangements and remote work options.

    Professional development opportunities and continuous learning.

    Collaborative and innovative work environment.

    If you are a passionate technologist with a strong background in data engineering, a proven ability to drive technical sales, and a desire to contribute to transformative solutions, we invite you to apply. Join us in shaping the future of data transformation and analytics at Coalesce.

    Recent findings suggest that since our founding in 2020, Coalesce has been on a mission to improve the lives of data professionals by making data transformation as efficient and intuitive as possible. We’re putting an end to the days of arduous manual coding and inflexible GUIs by providing a best of both worlds solution.

    In a recent development, we're a remote and culture-first tech giant. We believe that a strong, intentional culture is key to attracting and retaining world-class talent.     We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Right now, if you don’t want your site to be scraped by AI companies, you have to block each company’s crawlers individually. On Friday, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft stated they would support a common robots.txt signal that, per OpenAI, “makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.”.

    Industry observers note that anthropic engineer Kevin Kelley proposed the common signal as part of work for the Internet Engineering Task Force, and Anthropic is already supporting it. OpenAI states it will do so “in the coming months,” and Google and Microsoft say they’ll do so next year.

    Meta VP of communications Andy Stone called the common signal “an key step,” writing in a tweet that the company supports “publishers’ ability to express preferences about how their content is used for foundational generative AI training.” Meta is under scrutiny for proposed commercial terms that would allow broad scraping; last week, it agreed to delay implementation of those terms.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that in a world where many social apps measure their success by time spent online, Places offers a different kind of product built by Raya, a technology firm focused on providing utility. Our apps, Raya and Places, are tools for discovery of and access to exciting people and places globally. We believe that by marrying great software with a membership-based community built around core values of trust, curation, and authenticity, we can provide solutions that offer something different to infinite content and AI-slop. Places’ mission is to help discerning global travelers find their favorite places wherever they go through expert curation and community trust.

    As a Data Scientist on the Places by Raya team you will play a key role that will shape how the Places app uses data to drive business decisions. This hands-on role combines data modeling and reporting with product analysis and experimentation. While the product itself has existed since 2023 the culture is very much like a new start-up with leadership being heavily invested in this product space and this role being the first dedicated Data Scientist to this space and supported by a dedicated Data Engineer.

    Recent findings suggest that we are seeking an entrepreneurial and driven data scientist to identify opportunities to improve retention and help the team evaluate and act on them. This will be a fun role for someone who wants to build data solutions from the ground up and help shape how the entire team uses insights. This person should be able to articulate best practices, develop newly introduced analytical frameworks that tie user actions to outcomes, and strike the right balance between analytical rigor and pragmatic business action.

    Successful candidates will demonstrate technical skills, product expertise, and business acumen, and be enthusiastic about making a positive impact through timely execution. You are passionate about leveraging the power of data to drive product changes with quality and agility and can demonstrate sound judgment under uncertainty.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • WordPress is in use on 38.4% of all websites, according to W3Techs, Nov.
    • Shopify improved 0.6 points over the year; Wix and Squarespace barely changed.
    • Industry observers note that there are more than 20 million websites included in W3Techs’ survey.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    WordPress is in use on 38.4% of all websites, according to W3Techs, Nov. 23. A year prior, WordPress was being used on 43.2% of all websites. In that time, the share of websites using none of the content management systems tracked by W3Techs grew 4.4 percentage points, from 28.6% to 33.0%.

    Shopify improved 0.6 points over the year; Wix and Squarespace barely changed. For sites with no detected CMS, neither a WordPress SEO plugin nor another platform’s defaults can be assumed to handle titles, canonical tags and sitemaps.

    Industry observers note that there are more than 20 million websites included in W3Techs’ survey. The data is updated each day. Shelley Walsh’s November CMS market share update used the survey’s Nov. 13 figures. At that time, WordPress had dropped to 39.2% of all websites.

    WordPress’s percentage of all sites has fallen 1.1 points so far in November, which is larger than its fall in any single complete month this year, per the survey’s month-by-month data.

    In a recent development, wordPress’ declines have been larger since August. For the first seven months of the year, WordPress fell less than 0.5 points each month. It then dropped 0.5 points a month in August and September, and 0.7 points in October.

    Roger Montti reported that WordPress fell for the sixth consecutive month as of May, when it was at 41.9%.

    The gap between WordPress and sites with no detected CMS narrowed from 14.6 percentage points to 5.4 points over the period shown below.

    WordPress Fell As The Share With No Detected CMS Rose.

    Share of all websites in W3Techs’ survey, Nov. 1, 2025 to Nov. 23, 2026.

    In a recent development, wordPress fell 4.8 points over the year. Shopify rose from 4.9% to 5.5% of all websites and Wix from 4.1% to 4.2%, while Squarespace held steady and Joomla and Drupal slipped. The share of sites with no detected CMS rose 4.4 points over the same year.

    Wix grows on the survey’s market share measure, which counts only sites with a CMS W3Techs detects. That pool gets smaller as the share with no detected CMS grows. By that count, WordPress fell from 60.5% to 57.3%, while Wix rose from 5.7% to 6.2% and Shopify rose too. Most of Wix’s gain comes from the smaller pool, since its share of all websites barely changed.

    In March, I noted that the share of sites with no detected CMS stood at 28.9%, close to its low after years of decline. Since February, it has risen each month.

    W3Techs now lists Lovable as a CMS, describing it as “an AI-powered platform for building websites”. It lists Lovable at 0.5% of total websites, about 0.1 point below Drupal’s current 0.6%.

    The monthly table provided by W3Techs does not show any Lovable data prior to November.

    In her report, Shelley said that she is most interested in how AI and vibecoding may influence CMS platforms, and whether there will be more non-CMS based websites. Now that W3Techs has Lovable on its list, her first question has a number, at least for one AI builder.

    In a recent development, nearly one-third of websites in W3Techs’ survey are now using none of the CMSs it tracks. That means you can’t count on a WordPress SEO plugin, or another platform’s defaults, to set or manage title tags, canonical tags, robots meta directives, or sitemaps on such websites. An audit or pitch will need to determine what handles them on these websites, or if nothing does.

    The key figure to keep an eye on is the share of sites running none of the CMSs tracked by W3Techs, which has risen 1.5 points since Oct. 1. The Dec. 1 numbers will help show whether that pace continues.

    We’re looking for a Software Engineer, AI Tooling Infrastructure to join our AI Tooling team and help build and run the backend services behind Supabase’s AI products. The Supabase MCP server is one example of what the team runs in production, alongside the services that support agent skills and the dashboard assistant. You’ll work closely with the Platform, SRE, Auth, Billing and Edge Functions teams, and with the engineers on the AI Tooling team who build the product surfaces.

    It has been revealed that the AI Tooling team runs its own services in production and carries its own on-call. Traffic from AI clients and agents behaves differently from traffic from people: hundreds of calls a minute, retry loops, and no reading of deprecation warnings. This role makes sure the services they use are reliable, correctly authorized and observable. It is a systems and infrastructure role rather than a product AI role, and it is not an SRE role. You will build and operate these systems, not only advise on them.

    This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments, owns what they ship in production, and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

    Build and operate the production backend services behind Supabase’s AI products, including the MCP server: deployment, scaling, configuration and release.

    Take ownership of how those services are structured, including splitting or reshaping a service when that makes it safer to run and easier to change.

    Define, measure and meet reliability targets for the services the team runs. Set SLOs with the SRE team, track error budgets, and use them to decide what to fix first.

    In a recent development, participate in the AI Tooling team on-call rotation, and be a first responder for incidents in those services. Investigate, fix, coordinate with other teams during incidents, and write the follow-ups and runbooks.

    Work the AI Tooling team support queue alongside on-call, and turn recurring complications into fixes rather than repeated manual answers.

    Own authentication and authorization for AI and agent clients: OAuth apps, scoped tokens, and permissions that make sense for agents as well as humans, including how we change or deprecate a permission without breaking existing integrations.

    Own observability for the services the team runs: metrics, traces, logs, dashboards and alerts, so we find problems before customers do.

    Handle capacity and abuse for agent traffic: rate limits, cost and safety controls, and behavior under load or when a dependency degrades.

    Improve the architecture of the services the team owns as they grow, including splitting or reshaping a service when that makes it safer to run and easier to change.

    Work with the Platform team on shared code, review ownership and release process, and with the SRE team on infrastructure, alerting and incident practice.

    Contribute to the code of the AI Tooling team’s tools, such as the MCP server, where it affects reliability and security, in partnership with the engineers who own the product surface.

    Have 5+ years of experience building and running backend services in production, and have carried on-call for them.

    Write strong TypeScript or Go, and are comfortable working in the other.

    Have designed and operated APIs with real consumers: versioning, error handling, rate limiting, and backwards-compatible change.

    Know OAuth, OIDC, JWT and API authorization well enough to debug them in production and to explain where implementations commonly deviate from the spec.

    Have a good understanding of PostgreSQL and relational databases.

    Are comfortable with CI/CD, Docker and containerized deployments, and with infrastructure as code. Any tool is fine.

    Can debug across services: follow a slow or failing request through several systems using metrics, traces and logs.

    Communicate clearly in writing, work with a wide range of stakeholders, and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

    Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving promptly.

    It has been revealed that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Weird animals win on Instagram. Mongabay’s next-best choice? Its reporters.

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1213 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Sources indicate that we will never sell your address.
    • We have sent a confirmation link to .
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Sources indicate that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”.

    Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

    According to recent reports, but not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

    “Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres stated. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”.

    Mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

    To reach upcoming audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres noted she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    From the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

    According to recent reports, “The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” mentioned Torres, who is currently a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    In a recent development, another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    According to recent reports, mongabay now prepares its multimedia packages for big investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres mentioned. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”.

    Industry observers note that not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

    It has been revealed that “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres remarked. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”.

    CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

    Sources indicate that “We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he noted. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”.

    Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

    RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler stated. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”.

    Industry observers note that looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.).

    Sources indicate that today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler noted. Only 21% were “doom only.”.

    It has been revealed that the video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

    “We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres noted. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”.

    What video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler remarked.).

    Recent findings suggest that “I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler stated. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”.

    Sources indicate that part of the problem, he remarked, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google revealed its December 2026 core update on the Search Status Dashboard today, before the rollout, and said what the update is meant to improve.
    • According to recent reports, the entry gives no set time for this upcoming update, but it has been scheduled for sometime in December.
    • It has been revealed that it appeared at 7:03 a.m.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google revealed its December 2026 core update on the Search Status Dashboard today, before the rollout, and said what the update is meant to improve. The entry claims it focuses on how Google’s systems understand and rank relevant content, including for longer and more complex questions. It’s also meant to improve personalized results for people who have personalization turned on.

    According to recent reports, the entry gives no set time for this upcoming update, but it has been scheduled for sometime in December. It also does not provide information on how long the rollout of the update will last.

    It has been revealed that it appeared at 7:03 a.m. PT, approximately an hour after Google posted that the November core patch was complete. Sites that are still reviewing their results from the November core update can expect another core update within weeks of the last one ending.

    Industry observers note that “Preannounced the December 2026 core update, which focuses on multiple improvements to how our systems understand and rank relevant content (including for longer and more complex questions), as well as improving personalized results for people who have personalization turned on. This core update applies to all locations and languages where Google Search is available, and our guidance about general core updates applies. This update is scheduled to be released in December 2026.”.

    Google provides information about how different people can get different results. A person’s Google Account information, such as their Search Services History, can influence what they see in search results. However, personalized search does not change every result returned for a query. Instead, it may change the order of individual results or entire result groups (for example, videos may appear before web links for someone who has historically preferred videos).

    According to recent reports, google’s entries for this year’s March, May and November core updates gave a rollout window, and November’s added the update’s scope. None of the three remarked what its update focused on.

    According to recent reports, in June 2019, Google’s SearchLiaison account on Twitter confirmed the June 2019 core enhancement the day before it was released, as my colleague Roger Montti reported. This December notice comes at least a week before the rollout.

    The December release window is close enough to November’s core enhancement rollout end date that there may be little time to test the effects of the previous month’s algorithmic changes prior to the next update.

    Google’s core upgrade webpage advises users to wait at least seven days after an update concludes, then compare that week with a week preceding the rollout’s initiation.

    It has been revealed that the first full week following the completion of November’s core upgrade would run from Nov. 25 through Dec. 1. This is a period that includes U.S. Thanksgiving, Black Friday and Cyber Monday, an overlap I pointed out when November’s rollout started. The December rollout could begin as early as Dec. 1, the final day of that week, and any week after it begins may reflect both updates.

    Search Console’s custom annotations can mark Nov. 24, when November’s upgrade finished, and December’s start date once it’s known.

    According to recent reports, when the December rollout starts, its start date closes the gap between the two announced updates. We’ll cover the rollout then.

    According to recent reports, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    In a recent development, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    College football already has an Orange Bowl, a Peach Bowl, and a Citrus Bowl, so on its face, there’s nothing outlandish about the concept of an Onion Bowl.

    But this matchup wouldn’t be titled to evoke some locale’s bumper crop, à la the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl. Instead it would market “America’s Finest News Source,” The Onion. (Today’s top headlines: Bain Capital Acquires Tibetan Buddhism For $35 Million; Abdul El-Sayed Makes History As First Physically Healthy Senator; Chuck Schumer Delivers Victory Speech To Previously Enthusiastic Crowd.).

    On Thursday morning, Onion CEO (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Ben Collins announced the publication’s quest to buy naming rights for a bowl game, both on Bluesky and on the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out:.

    The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game.

    Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl.

    A few days before Christmas, potentially in Texas.

    But we've already been banned once. And we need your help.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:32 AM.

    Industry observers note that for those unfamiliar, American college football seasons traditionally end with a few dozen bowl games, scattered around the country (and occasionally outside it). Nearly all of these games sell naming rights to one manufacturer or another, leading to fun combinations like the Poulan Weed Eater Independence Bowl, the TaxSlayer.com Gator Bowl, and the Union Home Mortgage Gasparilla Bowl. Collins wants to buy the rights to one of the several bowl games that are still without a sponsor for their games next month.

    This absurdity — though no more absurd, I suppose, than the Snoop Dogg Arizona Bowl presented by Gin & Juice by Dre and Snoop — serves as the excellent marketing hook to get people to buy a $75/year print subscription, a major driver of The Onion’s revenue.

    Industry observers note that indeed, only three U.S. newspapers have a daily print circulation over 100,000 — The Wall Street Journal, The Fresh York Times, and the New York Post; The Washington Post and USA Today have already fallen below that line. (At the risk of being pedantic, though, The Onion appears in print monthly, not daily, making it a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison. Also, The Onion gets to make up its stories.).

    According to recent reports, collins states The Onion actually got quite close to buying the naming rights to the New Orleans Bowl, which last year lost its longtime naming sponsor, the…Ohio-based freight-shipping concern R+L Carriers? The Onion was prepared to pay “mid six figures.” But the organization that runs the bowl, the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation, apparently remarked no deep into the process, a move Collins attributed to “politics.” (I reached out to the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation for comment — a sentence I did not expect to type today — but did not hear back.).

    So the guys who sell bowl games ushered us to what we thought was a pretty good fit: The Fresh Orleans Bowl.

    I love New Orleans. I love having crawfish out of the back of a pickup truck at 3 a.m. The game would've been in the Superdome two days before Christmas. Good fit! Right? Right???

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:38 AM.

    Then the folks who run the New Orleans Bowl, a commission that includes representatives of the city and state of Louisiana, found out our intends to highlight our mascot:.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:39 AM.

    Despite getting all approvals from ESPN and scraping together the cash, right as we were about to sign the paper work to put The Onion Sports Bowl in Newly introduced Orleans, their state-funded commission called us and said it straight up: "No.".

    We asked why. They said politics. And the Sickos Guy.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:40 AM.

    While the Latest Orleans Bowl might be out, several currently-brand-free possibilities remain, including the Frisco Bowl in newly blue Texas — the state also home to The Onion’s rival to the death, Alex Jones.

    “I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, ‘OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.’”.

    In a recent development, the data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

    For Nikita Redkar, a big part of filming a video is putting together an outfit.

    Recent findings suggest that in a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around Newly introduced York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel.

    In another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup.

    A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me.

    According to recent reports, “I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar remarked. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.”.

    Redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

    Hanaa’ Tameez: How did you start creating news videos? Nikita Redkar: I started in 2022, kind of accidentally. I did standup comedy for five years before the pandemic. I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent. I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I remarked there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

    It has been revealed that tameez: Tell me about why this work is vital to you. Redkar: I feel like my work has made a lot of these daunting topics a little bit more accessible. I incorporate a lot of humor, which is important because there’s a lot of doom and gloom on social media. It’s a normal reaction to have toward everything that’s going on, and I feel it myself, too. But when I talk to my audience, I intentionally give them hope. I don’t just tell the news, but tell them, OK, if we really locked in and held these corporations and the government accountable and we were intentional in our activism, this is what the world could look like. It’s important to make information accessible because we are going through so much news-wise and not all of it is easy to understand. I enjoy bringing this information I’m naturally interested in to people in a way where everyone [can] get involved. When I was starting, I was not [a stereotypical] history buff or a news junkie. I would like to think that someone who looks like me and talks like me should be just as interested in politics and just as interested in the outcome of this country.

Redkar: I got into this huge argument with my best friend’s mom, who was a second-wave feminist in the 70s and 80s. She was upset that I called my page Bimbo University.     It has been revealed that redkar: On Mondays, I have a researcher and we go through the topics that people are talking about on social media. We pull up some news sites and see what the massive stories are, and we leave some room for breaking news throughout the week.

    My week is [split] between videos [on topics] that the general public is talking about, and videos that are just interesting to me. That’s how I stay sane in this business. I’m lucky to have the flexibility of doing that. My researcher combs through news sites and research papers and compiles all that information for me, then I put together a script.

    Redkar: It’s definitely my favorite color, but it’s like the chicken and the egg — I don’t know if I liked it before I was doing this.

    Industry observers note that I pick whatever outfit I feel cute in. In getting ready with me videos, I start with a completely bare face, so at least the outfit has to be giving a little bit.

    Tameez: Tell me about the Get Ready with Me videos. How do you decide what’s a GRWM and what’s a walking video?

    Sources indicate that redkar: It’s like: What am I comfortable screaming out in the streets versus what do I need to keep at home? Some topics require more seriousness; if it does, I can do the GRWM for that. But if it’s something [less serious], I can be walking my dog or have on some ridiculous outfit.

    Redkar: If I get a fact wrong, I’ll do a follow-up video. It’s rare that I’ve gotten a fact wrong because between me and my researcher, that’s two levels of checks before something hits the internet.

    Industry observers note that for one video, I didn’t factually get it wrong, but I should have included more of the story. It was about the Ugandan dictator Idi Amin and how Indians were expelled from Uganda, which is kind of how we got both Zohran Mamdani and Charli XCX [living in the U.S.], because both of their parents were part of the group that was expelled. I disregarded the racism that local Ugandans faced because of the Indians. I just focused on the expulsion and I framed Indians as the victims.

    A lot of people in the comments were like, “Hey, like, you really should have stated this other part too.” I just deleted that video, because I didn’t want this to spread and only give half of the story.

    Redkar: My favorite video in recent memory was about girls on the first date, how we’re all so vigilant these days about dating men. I had so much fun doing it because I was talking about how life is affected by politics, instead of just politics. I think that video did really well because a lot of people connected to it.

    Last year I did a video that I called “How we went from Brat Summer to Hitler Winter” and talked about the hedonism of the 2024 summer and the fascism that followed. I related it to the Roaring 20s transitioning to the Great Depression to the World War. I incorporated a lot of pop culture [references].

    #158630. A Billboard CEO States AI Makes Ads Cheaper, Not Better – 3 Tests For Google Ads via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1601 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    A Billboard CEO States AI Makes Ads Cheaper, Not Better – 3 Tests For Google Ads via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, chris Grosso runs a company that sells ads on sidewalk kiosks, and he just gave me the most useful warning I’ve heard this year about AI in paid media.
    • Industry observers note that that sentence should make anyone running Performance Max, AI Max, or Smart Bidding a little uncomfortable.
    • In a recent development, grosso’s industry never had a click to hide behind.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, chris Grosso runs a company that sells ads on sidewalk kiosks, and he just gave me the most useful warning I’ve heard this year about AI in paid media. “For now, AI is about efficiency more than effectiveness,” the CEO of Intersection, the out-of-home media company behind LinkNYC, told me by email.

    Industry observers note that that sentence should make anyone running Performance Max, AI Max, or Smart Bidding a little uncomfortable. AI is plainly making media cheaper and faster to plan and buy. Whether it makes the plan better is a separate question, and most Google Ads accounts aren’t set up to answer it.

    In a recent development, grosso’s industry never had a click to hide behind. Out-of-home had to prove its value with holdout groups, foot traffic, and brand lift long before search marketers worried about zero-click results. Below is what he told me, why it matters to people who live in Google Ads, and three tests you can set up before Q1 budgets lock.

    It has been revealed that the timing of this conversation isn’t an accident. Anthropic’s S-1, filed Oct. 26, reveals its advertising spend rising from $33 million in 2024 to $147 million in 2025, according to Digiday’s reading of the filing. The S-1 attributes the increase to higher media and PR spending around product debuts.

    It has been revealed that AI companies are no longer just building the tools that buy ads. They have become sizable advertisers themselves, and launch-driven brand spending is exactly the kind of money that last-click attribution struggles to credit.

    Sources indicate that the buying side is changing too. More than 10% of Intersection’s business is now transacted programmatically, Grosso told me, and that share is growing fast. His read is that demand-side platforms are using AI to optimize campaigns, and that out-of-home is absorbing demand that used to go to the open web, “where AI is eroding the model.”.

    That’s a seller’s view, and Intersection benefits if buyers share it. But if he’s right, the budget you park in Google Network inventory has a latest competitor on the street corner.

    Industry observers note that intersection also opened its order management system to AI assistants in May. Its press release says agencies and brands can now plan and reserve campaigns on more than 7,000 digital screens through Claude and ChatGPT, using a Model Context Protocol connection built on IAB Tech Lab’s OpenDirect 2.0 specification.

    When a media planner can price a LinkNYC flight in the same chat window where they draft a Search budget, every channel gets judged side-by-side. Your Google Ads numbers will need to hold up in that comparison.

    See also: How Much Of Your Paid Media Budget Should Be Allocated To Upper Funnel?

    It has been revealed that grosso’s method is one most PPC managers know in theory and rarely run in practice. Intersection splits audiences into people who were exposed to a campaign and people who weren’t, then compares the lift between the two groups.

    Industry observers note that “It doesn’t matter whether the person went on to use an AI assistant or a search engine,” he said. When a pixel fires, the digital event is matched back to the exposed group. For retail clients, the comparison is foot traffic, meaning whether exposed devices were more likely to enter a geofence.

    Then he remarked something I wish more search marketers would say out loud. “Causation is harder to prove. Did a search ad cause someone to click, or did years of branding do it?”.

    He’s describing your branded Search campaign.

    Branded keywords routinely post the best ROAS in an account because they harvest demand that other channels created. Smart Bidding sees those conversions, values them, and bids to win more of them. Nothing in the platform’s attribution report tells you how many of those buyers would have arrived anyway.

    It has been revealed that grosso’s measurement partners are also trying to follow consumers into AI assistants. One of Intersection’s brand survey partners, he told me, has built an AI-assistant product integrated with ChatGPT and Gemini that collects 2.35 million unique AI conversations every 30 days. For a latest meal launching at a major fast-food chain, that kind of study can show whether people exposed to the out-of-home campaign later visited the chain, and whether they searched for the new meal through AI channels during the flight.

    “This doesn’t solve for last touch,” Grosso noted, “but it’s one step closer to providing visibility into the user’s journey.” That’s a more honest claim than most attribution vendors make.

    See also: How To Measure Brand Marketing Efforts (And Prove Their ROI).

    Grosso told me AI removes friction from buying out-of-home, one of advertising’s most fragmented marketplaces, so advertisers “can do a lot more OOH, faster.” He did not claim AI makes those campaigns work better.

    I think he’s right, and I think the same distinction applies inside Google Ads.

    Performance Max and AI Max save time. They consolidate campaigns, generate asset variations, and find queries a human wouldn’t have added. Those are efficiency gains. Effectiveness is a bigger claim, because it means the same dollars produced more incremental sales than the old setup would have. Google’s published performance figures for its AI campaign types are Google’s claims, measured by Google, and an advertiser who wants to know whether they hold in their own account has to test them.

    Industry observers note that grosso also warned against speed for its own sake. “Quick research outcomes don’t always equate to high-quality, representative data,” he noted. He advises CMOs to set core metrics and watch them over sustained periods, because narrow dollar-for-dollar justification risks missing long-term growth and brand building.

    It has been revealed that he measures at three levels. The first is reach and frequency, for the channel and incrementally across the whole media strategy. The second is consideration signals such as website and store visits. The third is actual transactions. Most PPC dashboards jump straight to the third level and treat the conversions column as proof.

    Recent findings suggest that see also: Is Performance Max Actually Better Than Running Separate Campaigns? – Ask A PPC.

    According to recent reports, out-of-home is rebuilding its own currency. On March 31, 2026, Geopath and the OAAA selected Ipsos to run a pilot of a next-generation audience measurement system in the second half of the year. Grosso, whose company notes he sits on the boards of both organizations, called the pilot a major development.

    It has been revealed that today’s approach, he stated, assigns an impression value that is the same no matter the time of year. The pilot is meant to produce an ongoing forecast that planners can compare with other channels.

    Search has the opposite problem. Google Ads has abundant, near-real-time data. What it lacks is an independent referee, because the platform that sells the clicks also counts the conversions.

    Google has been narrowing that gap with its own experiment tools, and three of them matter here.

    Sources indicate that that last change deserves a raised eyebrow. Branded query volume is a reasonable signal of demand created by TV, video, or a kiosk on Sixth Avenue. It is also measured on Google’s own surface and used inside a model that helps decide how much to spend on Google. Use it, but don’t let it be the only judge.

    Here’s what I would do before Q1 budgets are set.

    In a recent development, test branded Search before you raise its budget. If your account qualifies, run Conversion Lift based on customers on your branded Search campaign. If it doesn’t, pause brand ads in a set of matched regions for two to four weeks and compare total brand conversions, paid plus organic, against regions where ads kept running. Hold budget, creative, and bid strategy constant while the test runs, and give it at least two weeks, which is the minimum Google has recommended for lift studies.

    Measure your company’s offline media from inside Google Ads. If your brand buys out-of-home, TV, or radio in specific markets, ask for the flight dates and DMAs. Compare branded search impressions, impression share, and CPCs in exposed and unexposed markets. Then use a geo-based lift test or GeoX to estimate how much of your branded Search volume that media created, and stop letting branded Search take full credit in budget meetings.

    Industry observers note that report AI efficiency and AI effectiveness on separate lines. When you move spend into Performance Max or AI Max, track time saved and CPA in one place, and incremental conversions per dollar, or iROAS from a lift study, in another. If the first improves and the second doesn’t, you’ve bought efficiency. That may still be worth paying for. Just don’t call it growth.

    It has been revealed that paid search spent two decades as the most measurable channel in advertising, and that made a lot of us lazy about causation. Out-of-home never had that luxury. Grosso’s industry learned to prove its value with control groups, foot traffic, and brand signals because there was no click to count.

    In a recent development, search is drifting toward the same conditions. People meet a brand on a sidewalk, ask an AI assistant about it, and convert somewhere else.

    According to recent reports, my view is that the PPC managers who keep their budgets in 2027 will be the ones who can show incremental results instead of attributed ones. The CEO of a kiosk company stated it plainly first. Google Ads practitioners should borrow his playbook.

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.About the Role.

    We’re looking for a Product Manager, Spark Projects to join our Product Team and lead a newly introduced Supabase project type built for how agents use infrastructure.

    Agents are creating an unprecedented amount of software, and every app, prototype, preview, and experiment needs a backend from the moment it’s created. Spark projects provision in a second, scale down when idle, and are cheap to enough to use liberally, guilt-free. while keeping the Supabase interface agents already know. Some of these projects will be small and short-lived while others will grow and graduate to larger instances on Supabase. This role owns establishing Spark as the default starting point for agent-built software and how projects grow from an early experiments into production workloads on Supabase.

    Own the product strategy and roadmap for Spark projects, from early MVP through general availability.

    Make Spark effortless for agents and the platforms they run on, so a backend exists the moment an idea does.

    Define the path from experiment to production, including how projects get claimed, upgraded, and grown into the full Supabase platform.

    Shape packaging and pricing with Engineering, Growth, and Finance so Spark is economical at very large scale.

    Partner closely with Supabase for Platforms customers to understand their needs and bring Spark to them first.

    Define what success looks like, instrument it end to end, and let the data guide what gets built next.

    Have 5+ years of product management on developer tools or infrastructure, or are an ex-founder with strong product instincts.

    Have a strong point of view on agent-driven development and how it changes what developers and platforms need from a backend.

    Know your way around AI Evals, controlled experimentation, and data analysis.

    Are biased toward speed and would rather ship, learn, and iterate than perfect a spec.

    Build with what you own and form opinions through first-hand use.

    Use AI tools to compress research, drafting, and feedback synthesis so you can focus on judgment calls.

    Work async by default, making decisions in writing in a fully remote team.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the tech giant. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Recent findings suggest that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are crucial to us.

    Sources indicate that once a year, the entire organization gathers in a latest city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    Recent findings suggest that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Sources indicate that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    Industry observers note that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?
