    Stations in New Hampshire, Wisconsin, Massachusetts, and Utah all climbed in our regular ranking of public radio stations between July and September.

    Recent findings suggest that more than a year ago, NHPR reporter Todd Bookman started asking questions about “an irregular personnel maneuver” involving the chief justice of Newly introduced Hampshire’s Supreme Court. Bookman’s reporting ultimately became “Exhibit A” in the ethics probe that led to the justice’s resignation in September.

    The bombshell resignation news was NHPR’s biggest story in September — and of 2026 to date. The story helped push NHPR up several spots in our regular ranking of public radio websites. NHPR saw visits rise 22% that month, according to Similarweb visit figures compiled by Nieman Lab.

    RELATED ARTICLECollaborations and primary elections boosted traffic to public media sites this quarterNeel DhaneshaJuly 29, 2026At the very top of the list, not much moved. The Chicago Sun-Times, owned by Chicago Public Media, held onto the top spot, followed by Gothamist (from WNYC) and Minnesota Public Radio. As Nieman Lab senior writer Joshua Benton wrote when introducing the rankings, which we’ve also done for local newspapers and local nonprofit news sites, not all markets are created equal. Public radio stations serving major metropolitan areas with lots of college graduates have a bigger potential audience than stations serving smaller communities and areas with fewer resources. And, of course, Similarweb provides an estimate; internal metrics may differ. Still, the rankings are a valuable window into some industry-wide trends, and often an opportunity to highlight local news organizations punching above their weight.

    It has been revealed that like several public media sites on our list, election season provided a bump to NHPR. Latest Hampshire held its primary on Sept. 8 and the statewide public radio station saw a traffic boost from results pages and campaign coverage, said NHPR director of audience engagement Casey McDermott. She described September as a solid month, not an outlier. “But what makes September an exceptionally cool case study is that it reflects two fundamentals at the heart of our mission: a commitment to fresh, local reporting and a renewed internal investment in digital publishing,” McDermott said. “[Bookman’s piece] wasn’t just a standard breaking news item — it was the culmination of months of meticulous accountability reporting,” McDermott added. On the audience side, McDermott said that, in addition to a boost from NHPR’s partners at NPR and Google News, the chief justice story benefited from X (formerly known as Twitter). A post by NHPR president and CEO Jim Schachter caught on and inspired “a stream of supportive comments about the importance of local journalism.” BREAKING: Fearless reporting by New Hampshire Public Radio results in the resignation of the chief justice of the New Hampshire Supreme Court. #NHPolitics https://t.co/6DtIeEIwdp — Jim Schachter (@jimschachter) September 15, 2026 WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. WBUR had the biggest raw gain of any station in September. Tiffany Campbell, WBUR’s executive editor for digital audience and news, said organic search traffic and Google Discover helped. “We’ve been working on building out many referral streams,” Campbell said, “but in early September Google delivered a lot of organic search audience via a couple of strong stories.” “Our referral diversification aims to be less reliant on Google organic search but it’s also important to take advantage when it delivers,” she added. Those strong stories? An explainer on the insanity defense during jury deliberations in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, results from the Massachusetts primary held on Sept. 1, and a Here & Now interview with Associated Press photographer Richard Drew — who took the “Falling Man” photo — on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. All three stories drew both local and national readers, Campbell said. Campbell credited the steady rise in traffic to “things we’re always doing: in-depth local coverage, comprehensive reporting on a closely watched election (which was an early indication of interest in the general election in November) and relevant enterprise reporting.” The Milwaukee-based WUWM was the fastest climber in the top 25 this quarter. The station nearly doubled its visits between June and September, rising in our ranking from No. 31 to No. 15. According to Similarweb, the station’s visits rose 32% in August and by another 17% in September. Michelle Maternowski, WUWM audience innovation manager, said the surge started with Wisconsin’s August 11 primary. “We published our Voter Guide in time for that and saw a decent amount come to our meet the candidate posts,” she said. Readers were especially interested in news and information on the lesser-known races. “We see lots of traffic to the down ballot, statewide races — like state treasurer and secretary of state.” And then there’s the gift that keeps on giving. Published in 2019, WUWM’s segment on the 150th birthday of the periodic table still ranks “really high in search results.” “I think once the school year started up again, a lot of students were searching their periodic tables,” Maternowski said. “It is very silly that this story continues to get so much traffic.” If you only look at the top 25 stations, you’ll miss some impressive jumps. The Salt Lake City-based KUER, for example, took the biggest leap in ranking of any station in July. The station’s visits rose 122% that month, according to Similarweb’s numbers. “The numbers don’t lie,” Jim Hill, digital manager in the KUER newsroom, confirmed. “July was a monster for us.” Hill had expected a “plateau or small retreat” after a record year in 2025 — which included the Charlie Kirk killing and a shooting at a No Kings Protest in Utah. Instead, the news site has been ahead of last year’s pace. Total customers are up 19% over last year, even after attempts to filter out bots, and social media referrals falling by 54%. (Hill noted the station’s social media producer was laid off and that KUER is attempting to “pivot to video/reels.”) The station saw “some runaway Google Discover success” last year but, in 2026, clicks from Google Discover are “less than half” of its 2025 figures. Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds. KUER also grew its “owned” email audience and drove 34% more users to the website compared to 2025, according to Hill. All in all, July was “very hit-heavy,” Hill said. The top 10 stories — led by Donald Trump’s decision to dramatically shrink two Utah national monuments — accounted for 64% of the month’s views. The station also saw a major boost from NPR, including multiple stories from a week-long hearing in the Charlie Kirk case. “Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill said. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%. Two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit. “We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill said. “It always hits with the audience.” Sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story.     Instead, the news site has been ahead of last year’s pace. Total customers are up 19% over last year, even after attempts to filter out bots, and social media referrals falling by 54%. (Hill noted the station’s social media producer was laid off and that KUER is attempting to “pivot to video/reels.”) The station saw “some runaway Google Discover success” last year but, in 2026, clicks from Google Discover are “less than half” of its 2025 figures. Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds. KUER also grew its “owned” email audience and drove 34% more users to the website compared to 2025, according to Hill.

    Recent findings suggest that all in all, July was “very hit-heavy,” Hill mentioned. The top 10 stories — led by Donald Trump’s decision to dramatically shrink two Utah national monuments — accounted for 64% of the month’s views. The station also saw a major boost from NPR, including multiple stories from a week-long hearing in the Charlie Kirk case.

    “Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill remarked. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%.

    Recent findings suggest that two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit.

    “We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill remarked. “It always hits with the audience.”.

    Sources indicate that sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story.

    #158585. OpenAI Has No Looks For Prompt-Level ChatGPT Ads Reports via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (638 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    OpenAI Has No Looks For Prompt-Level ChatGPT Ads Reports via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (638 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • OpenAI doesn’t plan to provide ChatGPT advertisers with reports showing the prompts or inferred intent behind their ads.
    • Three executives who run OpenAI’s ad system told Adweek that ChatGPT ads are matched to search queries written by the organization’s own AI agent.
    • OpenAI’s basics page for advertisers explains that Ads Manager Beta reporting currently includes impressions, clicks, spend, CTR, average CPC, average CPM and conversions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    OpenAI doesn’t plan to provide ChatGPT advertisers with reports showing the prompts or inferred intent behind their ads. When Adweek asked whether advertisers could expect such reports, Vijaye Raji, OpenAI’s CTO of applications, noted they should not expect them.

    Three executives who run OpenAI’s ad system told Adweek that ChatGPT ads are matched to search queries written by the organization’s own AI agent. Advertisers don’t see those queries, only aggregate results.

    OpenAI’s basics page for advertisers explains that Ads Manager Beta reporting currently includes impressions, clicks, spend, CTR, average CPC, average CPM and conversions.

    OpenAI’s “About this ad” panel tells customers why they saw an ad and what performance data advertisers receive.

    OpenAI’s ad system begins by creating one or more search queries based upon buying intent determined from the conversation, per the tech giant’s ads engineering post published Oct. 21 by Ritendra Datta and Karthik Gopalratnam. OpenAI calls the model that creates these search queries the orchestrator. Using these search queries, the ad system retrieves candidate ads, filters them, scores them and identifies the top candidates to be entered into an auction to set the price and select the winner. Returning no ad is called “an ordinary, successful outcome” in the post.

    As described in the post, if a user asks about a two-day Yosemite trip and then about a shoe brand’s new product lines, the ad system may create a query representing that conversation such as “shoes appropriate for hiking trip,” even though the user did not connect the two questions.

    According to the post, when ads personalization is turned on, the orchestrator will also consider “nonsensitive information about the user’s past conversations.”.

    Industry observers note that chatGPT people in the European Economic Area and Switzerland will not have access to personalized ads at first, according to OpenAI’s ads FAQ for users. Brooke Osmundson covered the engineering post in October.

    Advertisers share context hints about where an ad might fit, and OpenAI indicates these hints help guide matching without determining it.

    OpenAI’s context hints guide states:.

    In a recent development, “Hints are not targeting rules or delivery instructions. They do not guarantee that your ad will appear for particular conversations, audiences, or situations, and they cannot enforce geographic limits, schedules, or exclusions.”.

    The basics page also notes that hints “are not exact-match keywords.” Negative Phrases help qualifying advertisers limit where their ads appear, for “narrow placement requirements specific to their brand’s own policies.” The option is not necessarily available to every advertiser.

    Industry observers note that google explains that for some AI searches, the search terms provided in Google Ads reporting reflect the user’s intent rather than the exact query. According to Google’s ad group prioritization page, for searches done through Lens, AI Mode, AI Overviews and autocomplete, “the search term shown in your reporting represents the best approximation of the user’s intent.” Brooke posted about Google’s patch to that page in May.

    OpenAI does not list a search terms report on its basics page.

    Recent findings suggest that chatGPT advertisers can determine what a campaign delivered, but they cannot see the conversations or queries that led to the results. Click-based and conversion-based campaigns can use the conversion tracking OpenAI supports through Ads Manager Beta. The basics page also describes how UTM parameters added to landing page URLs persist on ad clicks.

    OpenAI recommends writing your context hints in terms of customer needs and scenarios instead of listing keywords. Also, use OpenAI’s product controls where available to restrict delivery by geography.

    According to recent reports, openAI claims in its ads FAQ for users that it “may explore additional measurement insights over time while continuing to protect user privacy.” OpenAI sends fresh feature announcements by email to account holders. Check the reporting list on the basics page for updates.
